items.body: Nothing is quite what it seems on Zawsze coś. Ben Bekele is not, in fact, a single musician but the collective identity adopted by Hubert Zemler, Kamil Piotrowicz and Igor Wiśniewski. Nor is Bekele a surname in the Western sense. In Ethiopia, where hereditary family names are not traditionally used, Bekele—meaning “he has grown” or “he has flourished”—is simply a personal name, one that immediately unsettles assumptions about identity. Zemler has long enjoyed these conceptual sleights of hand. “The Life and Death of Ben Bekele,” released on the Portrety compilation (2019) by U Know Me Records, first introduced this fictional figure, while Gostak & Doshes (2014) borrowed its title from the famous linguistic phrase “the gostak distims the doshes.” The album’s cover, assembled from photographs taken by Zemler’s parents during their travels in Africa, already pointed towards the persistence of family memory. The blurred photograph on Zawsze coś, also taken by his father during a trip to Ethiopia in the mid-1980s, returns to the same personal archive, suggesting that these images continue to resurface in different forms. Yet Zawsze coś has remarkably little to do with Ethiopia itself. Instead, it reflects on the way memories become family mythology. Zemler’s father returned from Africa with photographs, stories, two small drums and the memory of a boy named Bekele teaching him a traditional song. Four decades later these fragments re-emerge, not as ethnographic reconstruction but as the starting point for an entirely personal musical language. The record consistently resists exoticism and refuses to turn biography into narrative. Rhythm provides its structural foundation. “La Clave en medio de la nada” hints at ritual before “R-4” answers with a precision that feels almost architectural, carefully avoiding the familiar vocabulary of free improvisation. “Niosą” introduces a more reflective register, but “Phillip Jeffries” quietly redirects the entire album. Named after David Bowie’s enigmatic Twin Peaks character, forever suspended between dream and reality, the piece invites the same uncertainty that Lynch famously condensed into the question: “We live inside a dream.” From there, the title track “Zawsze coś” changes course once again before arriving at “Linoleum (Shining).” Whether the title alludes to the famous hexagonal carpet pattern from Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining remains deliberately ambiguous, but the reference would be entirely in keeping with the album’s fascination with memory, dreams and unstable realities. That refusal to stabilise meaning is precisely what gives the album its character. Zawsze coś never asks the listener to distinguish fact from invention, memory from fantasy, or autobiography from fiction. Instead, it inhabits the uncertain space where all of these overlap, allowing rhythm, recollection and imagination to coexist without demanding resolution. Hubert Zemler by Krzysztof Pawłowski To shed some light on the production process for the album, Hubert Zemler kindly agreed to answer a few questions for us by email. Ben Bekele begins with a memory that may not even be entirely reliable: an Ethiopian song your father brought back from a trip in the 1980s, filtered through decades of recollection and imagination. How do you navigate the space between personal memory, family mythology, and cultural reference when building the world of Ben Bekele? At what point does memory become composition? First and foremost, I must say that this story is true. However, its influence on the music and the entire concept of the Ben Bekele project is only symbolic. In my ideal world, the music should speak for itself, and descriptions should be superfluous. However, this would require erudition and contextual knowledge from listeners, which is impossible in the current online reality. A properly told story adds context to the music, increasing the chance that someone will reflect and pause. In this case, memory is simply a part of my identity. Ben Bekele is not a concept album, but a record of my current emotional state. Given that Ben Bekele originated from such a personal source—a childhood memory of your father, his stories from Ethiopia, and a melody that resurfaced decades later from your subconscious—what made you decide that this project should become a collaboration rather than a solo record? What did Kamil Piotrowicz and Igor Wiśniewski bring to the music that allowed you to expand such an intimate and autobiographical idea into something larger than your own memory? After many solo albums, I wanted to tap into the imagination and energy of younger musicians. On the album Zawsze coś (Always Something), I decided to utilize the talents of two wonderful improvisers: Kamil Piotrowicz and Igor Wiśniewski. My part is limited to ethnic rhythms, which have always fascinated me. Interestingly, although I listen to a lot of Ethiopian music, none of the compositions are based on the music of this region. I gave Kamil and Igor quite specific guidelines on what I expected from the final result, but left them free to choose the means to achieve their goal. I wanted to avoid free jazz improvisation, with solos and formal chaos. So I told my companions: every note should be the final note: “I don’t want to hear the creation process, only the finished composition.” They fulfilled this task brilliantly. Thanks to this, we composed compositions together that we perform in a similar format live and avoided the trap of a “free improv” album, which is a stream-of-consciousness recording of improvising musicians. The title Zawsze coś is a wonderfully ambiguous Polish expression—part resignation, part optimism, suggesting that even when things fall short, something remains. Why did you choose it as the album’s title, and does it reflect the emotional atmosphere of the record or perhaps the collaborative process between yourself, Kamil Piotrowicz, and Igor Wiśniewski? The title has nothing to do with the creative process. As you yourself pointed out, it’s wonderfully ambiguous. It could be “oh no, not that” or “at least that much,” but it’s also a phrase that symbolically emphasizes that life is a constant movement and transformation. As a parent, but also someone caring for an elderly mother, working in the uncertain profession of a freelance artist, I have a lot of problems to solve. Just when it seems like everything’s taken care of, something always comes up. Always something. Rhythm seems to function as the album’s primary organizing principle, often taking precedence over melody or harmonic development. Tracks such as “Niosą” and “La Clave en medio de la nada” feel almost trance-like in the way they build momentum through repetition and subtle variation. What interests you about rhythm as a form-generating force, and how did the three of you develop this collective rhythmic language? I’ve already partially answered this question in point 2. Drums are my instrument because they are close to the primary role of music (and art in general) – to transport the listener momentarily to another dimension. Beyond reality, to distance themselves from everyday matters. One of the album’s most intriguing titles is “Phillip Jeffries,” referencing the mysterious Twin Peaks character who becomes untethered from ordinary reality while pursuing forces beyond human comprehension. What drew you to Jeffries as a point of reference, and do you see parallels between his disappearance into an unknown realm and the way this music often seems to move between concrete reality, memory, dream, and imagination, especially since this track in particular seems to be the most mysterious on the album? You’ve essentially partially answered this question yourself. You understood my intentions very well. Phillip Jeffries is the one who knocks on us from our dreams. It’s not without significance that this character is played by David Bowie, who is a great inspiration to me on many levels. The universe created by David Lynch is like a cure for the madness of the modern world. We all live in a dream – but who is the dreamer? (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Transglobal Underground reworked the Bengali folk song “Beautiful Lotus” into “The Seahorse”, out on 9 July as their second single of the year. Sheema Mukherjee sings lead and plays sitar. The song hopes for a love it knows it won’t get: the dawn dew on the lotus stirs the feeling, morning light admits it is impossible, and the singer holds onto the hope regardless: “even though I know this, I still hope“. The collective helped build the template British world-electronic music followed. Signed to Nation Records, they ran tabla, oud and dub basslines through club beats when few others were, and “Temple Head” carried that sound to a mass audience after Coca-Cola used it in a 1996 Olympics advert. Their debut Dream of 100 Nations introduced Natacha Atlas, lead singer on their first four albums, and 2008’s Moonshout won them the BBC Radio 3 Award for World Music. Tim Whelan and Hamid Mantu have held the core together across a line-up that has run from studio team to DJ crew to today’s five-piece live band. Mukherjee trained in Hindustani classical sitar under her uncle, the sitarist Nikhil Banerjee, and has played with the group since 1998. On “The Seahorse” her sitar and her voice carry the melody together, the Bengali source folded into their electronic production. You can stream and buy “The Seahorse” on Bandcamp, where two more remixes wait alongside it.   The post Daily Discovery: Transglobal Underground – The Seahorse appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — This is simultaneously being posted to my blog, Scott's Song by Song Spotlights.Clicked 5, but close at 4.5 stars! 4 is too low.The Bardic Depths are a UK prog band led by multi-instrumentalist/composer Dave Bandana and American Historian Brad Birzer (doing spoken word narratives) . It sprung from an earlier project that the two had entitled Birzer Bandana. They released their eponymous first album in 2020. There were a number of notable guest musicians such as Peter Jones (Camel/Tiger Moth Tales), Tim Gehrt (Streets, Steve Walsh Band), Gareth Cole (Fractal Mirror) and Robin Armstrong (Cosmograf) who contributed to the album. Jones, Gehrt, and Cole are now official members. Birzer is still a primary lyricist, but not listed as a band member. The second album came in 2022 with "Promises of Hope", while the third album "What We Really Like in Stories' dropped in 2024. Today, I'll be checking out the 4th album, "Some Things are Worth Remembering" which will be released this Friday, August 7, 2026. The album came courtesy of Dave Bandana. I receive no additional compensation, and always call it like I hear it. As usual, this is a cold listen.Here is the line-up:- Dave Bandana / vocals, keyboards, bass- Peter Jones / vocals, clarinet, alto saxophone- Gareth Cole / 12-string, electric & acoustic guitars, vocals- Tim Gehrt / drums, vocalsLet's jump in!Track 1 - Islands (8:37)This begins with a rumbling sound and orchestral synths, joined by a clean guitar. The vocals begin soon after. The opening vocals conclude with the album's title being quoted. A jaunty woodwind section plays a rhythmic pattern soon joined by drums and bass. Just before the 3 minute point, the tempo increases, and soon after the music becomes more intense. Killer lead guitar from Cole! After things come back down, Jones gives us a sax feature. This section is jazzy, with Cole & Jones trading licks. Bandana provides a moving bass line and synth beds while Gehrt keeps the beat lively. Vocals return after 5 minutes. The keyboard string tones sound like a mellotron. The overall vibe is very dreamy and floaty. Great opening track!Track 2 - Fallen Leaves (3:03)This shorter track starts with acoustic guitar and sax. Beautiful wordless harmony vocals join in before long. Just before the one-minute mark the rhythm section joins in. This is a great chill-out track; very calming and peaceful. The playing and singing are wonderful. The production is rich and warm. Nice track!Track 3 - Arribabok (5:29)A guitar melody supported by keys starts things off here. Some percussion rhythms join in. The vocals come in sounding intentionally distant with an effect. This has a "world music" feel to it; sort of African. The song slowly evolves as it progresses. The instrumental parts take the bulk of the content here as the vocals have dropped out for much of the middle section. They begin to fade back in during Jones' sax solo. This reminds me a bit of something Peter Gabriel would do. The vocals take back over with effects still in place at the ending. Super cool track.Track 4 - October Sun (8:13)A slow guitar melody supported by bass & keys kicks this one off. Vocals soon join in. Great harmonies just after one minute. The beat kicks in at around 1:50. I like the bass fills. The vocal harmonies are the star here, though; they really shimmer. I like the refrain that begins between 3:30-4:00 ? "Let it shine, let it shine, until the sun falls from the sky!" At 5:15, there is an a cappella line, then an instrumental guitar break takes over with a great solo from Cole. A wonderful sax solo from Jones follows. Harmonized guitar lines follow. The rhythm section is keeping it bouncy. This one is going to be an ear worm! Fantastic track! Probably my favorite so far on the album.Track 5 - From Empty Trees (4:41)A big, dramatic synth-led intro commences activities here, and it gets even bigger after 15 seconds with a choir-like sound. Beautifully done! At around 30 seconds, we get a funky riff that somehow reminds me of Lynyrd Skynyrd's "Saturday Night Special" (never mentioned them in a prog review before!). Following that, though, the synth solo is straight-up Camel influences, really cool! This is all over the place, but in a good way! The funky groove returns for a fusion-esque guitar solo from Cole. This is shaping up to be an awesome instrumental track! I love it; another favorite track contender. Great dynamics!Track 6 - A View (6:17)This one starts with a mystical vibe. At about 25 seconds though, a strong 6-8 shuffle takes over. There are some meter shifts as the vocals enter and proceed through the first verse. The mellotron tones remind me of the Moody Blues; as in "The Other Side Of Life" mixed with their 70s mellotron sound. Jones' sax solo kicks off with a fabulous high note. Cole briefly takes over on guitar at 4:00. I love the vocals around 5:40! Another terrific track!Track 7 - Harder to See (4:10)This one is also in 6-8 but has a very different feel from "A View" . I believe Bandana is the lead singer. He sometimes reminds me of John Wetton or even a bit of former Genesis singer Ray Wilson on "Calling All Stations"; I like it! I love the guitar and keyboard lines in the instrumental break. This may be where Jones plays the clarinet. Cool track, very jazzy.Track 8 - Rewind (9:21)This is the longest track on the album so I will call it the closing epic. A gentle piano and acoustic 12-string support the vocals as the song begins. Wonderful harmonies enter at about 35 seconds. The lyrics wish that the narrator could "rewind his brain". This reminds me a little of Spock's Beard's "June" from a vocal standpoint. Nice guitar solo from Cole after the 3-minute mark. I like the call and response vocal section following the instrumental break. The music completely changes at around the 5 minute point. It becomes dreamy and floaty. Flute is not listed for Jones, but I believe he is playing it here. There are many layers to the soundscape here. Vocals begin to re-emerge at around the 8-minute point saying "Rewind" in harmony. This is a very mellow, ethereal ending to this wonderful album.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:Wow, 2026! What a year in prog. Here's another one that should be in the conversation as one of the finest prog albums in 2026. The production is impeccable, and the arrangements are beautiful. This is more on the mellow, pastoral side of prog, but it still has some rocking moments. I highly recommend to fans of Camel, and The Moody Blues. I give this a 4.5 out of 5 stars.

items.body: Review by Grumpyprogfan — The second release by Domi and JD is out, and oh my, it's weird. There is no doubt that they are talented musicians, but the compositions are lacking, for me, on this release. However, I do enjoy "Concertino" (best tune), "Epilogue", and most of "Lovely Masquerade." As for the sonics...The drums sound like JD is hitting shoe boxes with his hands. Overhead, like a fort, the boxes are surrounded with packing blankets and one mic is outside the blankets recording his performance. Then, he runs that take through a cheap distortion pedal. These are the worst sounding attempt at recording drums I've ever heard! Why? It is very fatiguing on the ears. The music is a combo of EDM, hip-hop, with jazzy and classical bits thrown in. Most songs are at the same tempo and they all sound similar. There is no verse or chorus to be found, just a spewing of free music mixed with cosmic dust, and lots of layered processed vocals. I don't get it. Definitely different, but not for me. I enjoyed their debut more.

items.body: Review by SSL1967 — With "Primadonna", recorded in 1978, their second and ultimately final album, Spheroe delivered one of the most accomplished hidden treasures of the French jazz-rock scene. Building upon their very good 1977 debut, the quartet sounds even more confident here, combining formidable musicianship with compositions that are intricate without ever sacrificing melody, groove or sheer listening pleasure.The band's greatest strength is its extraordinary interplay. Michel Perez's fluid, lyrical guitar constantly converses with G�rard Maimone's Fender Rhodes, Moog and piano, while bassist Rido Bayonne and drummer Patrick Garel form a remarkably supple rhythm section, capable of shifting effortlessly between jazz-rock complexity and infectious funk. Rather than becoming a succession of virtuoso showcases, "Primadonna" works as genuine ensemble music. Every instrumental voice serves the compositions.The magnificent "Arlecchino" is the album's centerpiece, nearly eight minutes of sophisticated fusion in which the melodic invention, rhythmic dexterity and instrumental dialogue of the band reach their peak. The title track is equally essential, balancing atmospheric delicacy with passages reminiscent of Brand X, while "Jeff" provides another superb demonstration of the group's elegant, highly melodic jazz-rock vocabulary.Although Spheroe disappeared shortly afterwards, "Primadonna" ensured their legacy. Alongside groups such as Zao and Cortex, Spheroe demonstrated that the French fusion scene could rival its British and American counterparts in technique, imagination and personality. An essential European jazz-rock album?and a fitting, frustratingly premature finale to a remarkable band.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A debut album often fails to fully reflect the potential a band will eventually reach, yet it does set a certain tone. Although Hawkwind was an English band, on "Hurry On Sundown" they sounded every bit as bluesy as American groups or even early Krautrock bands. Dave Brock played both guitar and harm�nica, an instrument quintessentially associated with the blues, evoking a distinctly American or German sound.By the time "The Reason Is?" begins, it is a different story... psychedelia and experimentation gain ground. It serves as an introduction to "Be Yourself", a track where Krautrock asserts itself, much like with so many British bands of the early 70s. They sound rough and raw; the songwriting is still developing, yet this is compensated for by an eagerness to play... to see where the music leads and, quite simply, to let themselves be carried away.When Nik Turner, the group's other key figure, enters with his saxophone, the missing piece falls into place. Hawkwind then takes on the yellow of the desert and the red of the sunset, the color of distorted guitar and the endless drumming that kicks off a ritual destined to last for years... a ritual that the wind would carry to all those willing to listen.Compared to better-crafted tracks like "Be Yourself," "Paranoia" (Parts 1 and 2) feels like a sketch, a work-in-progress demo with interesting ideas that still need polishing; there is a touch of the madness found in Van der Graaf Generator's H To He, Who Am The Only One. Michael "DikMik" Davies' electronic effects truly made a difference on "Seeing It As You Really Are," launching the track into a journey with no fixed destination... yet, fortunately, the bass, guitar, and saxophone wove together a certain musical coherence that brought order to the chaos. After all, not all chaos is art."Mirror of Illusion" is a little gem that begins with a slightly off-key sound, a brilliant touch, before settling into a 1960s British pop atmosphere with echoes of early Pink Floyd. It then transitions into a somewhat cosmic jam session reminiscent of the Grateful Dead, while the vocals brought to mind the early solo work of Steve Hillage.And so it fades out... accompanied by an echo and stereo maracas that foreshadow the ceremonies to unfold within this established setting, a landscape spanning various countries and continents that ultimately served to define the band itself.

items.body: Review by Logan — Blue Morpho from Radiohead founder and guitarist Ed O'Brien has been a major grower for me. When Ifirst heard it over a month ago, it was roughly a 3.89 star album for me. The first more peacefulhalf appealed much more to me than the more upbeat later tracks, but I came to love the whole thingand how eclectic it is. I was considering giving it a very strong four stars (more like a 4.45) when I was getting ready to review it, but after several more spins today (now about ten total,it's quite a short album by my 90s up standards) I feel like it really revealed itself for themasterpiece that it is, and it is an album that I know will continue to appeal to me.I am a big fan of Radiohead, and the album A Moon Shaped Pool is what made me a big fan ofRadiohead, and that Radiohead album does remind me of Blue Morpho. I also am a fan of The Smile,rate it highly, and it has some of my very favourite Radiohead related music such as "BendingHectic" and "Pana-Vision", but Mr. O'Brien's album exceeds The Smile's albums for me. It feels morespiritual in a sense, warm, down-to-earth and like it has more of a heart. The first track, "Incantations", was love at first listen. The folk qualities remind me of NickDrake, who is one of my very favourite artists, with Pink Moon. It also is hypnotic, quitepsychedelic, and brings to my mind Popol Vuh with a spiritual eastern vibe (think David Bowe's"Blackstar"). I love the acoustic pasterns and background vocals in this.The second track "Blue Morpho" immediately became one of my top tracks of the year. This isgorgeous! The gentle acoustics and swirling strings are bliss. Again I get Nick Drake qualitiesfrom this, but this time more the lushness and fragile beauty of the debut album. It also brings tomy mind music from the amazing Third by Portishead."Sweet Spot" also really hits the spot, and again I mention Nick Drake. In fact it is the most NickDrake of any of any of the tracks. It reminds me of "Fruit Tree" and has a similar kind of fragilemelancholy. So beautiful. It rather reminds me of some of the most beautiful music from later AIR.And then the violin melody is reminiscent of the piano in Westworld music composed by Ramin Djawadi.With "Teachers" the music moves more from Psychedelic Folk to Psychedelic Rock and Krautrock. Ithas a very motorik rhythm a la NEU! and especially reminds me of Can with music like "Vitamin C"."Teachers" is quite funky and has experimental electronic qualities. It offers a big sonic release,and it offers contrast with earlier music.With "Solfeggio" we are into ambient territory, like this could be released by WARP records, and Ilove the respite offered by this dreamy atmospheric music. It brings to mind Kosmische Musik,Cluster and Brian Eno and it brings to my mind Oneohtrix Point Never's tape manipulations.We then have another ambient track with "Thin Places". This has a haunting dreamy quality. It'svery ethereal. Shabaka Hutchings flute stylings make this short ambient track."Obrigado" is a wonderful uplifting closer, and with much contrast in different parts. The firstpart brings to my mind some of the ebullience of Fishmans dub ("Thank You"), and then it starts tomove in a Funkadelic "Maggot Brain" direction. This, the longest track, and sprawling though it is,id such a perfect track, kind of in a similar way that Sufjan Steven's "Impossible Soul" is whilesounding more Stevens' "Djohariah" than that due to similar "Maggot Brain" parallels. Quite Stevens2010 I might say. The guitar has a soulful bluesy quality that I love.This grower album definitely has reached five star album status for me over time and spins and is myfavourite album so far this year along with Boards of Canada's Inferno. Its atmospheric blend ofFolk, Krautrock, funky music and Post-Rock is perfect for my tastes, and this has become myfavourite Radiohead related release. While O"Brien was named one of the greatest guitarists of alltime by Rolling Stone, this is not music I would recommend to guitar hero types. This is morefocused on nuanced soundscapes, and atmospheric and textural depth.I am proud to have brought this album to this site, and I expect it to continue to rank very highlyon my list.

items.excerpt: The end is the beginning With a different name Laughter in sheets of metal Cutting through a memory of stone Crush of Souls has always carried himself like a man who missed the last train, stole a delivery van, and decided the road ahead probably merged into a bassline. items.body: The end is the beginning With a different name Laughter in sheets of metal Cutting through a memory of stone Crush of Souls has always carried himself like a man who missed the last train, stole a delivery van, and decided the road ahead probably merged into a bassline. On Captive Youth, his third full-length album, mastermind Charles Rowell turns that perpetual displacement into nine tracks of industrial dance music built for warehouses, bruised romances, and people who have memorized every fire exit in Europe. Rowell has spent years moving through Crocodiles, Flowers of Evil, Issue, and assorted corners of the international punk underground. Captive Youth treats that history as fuel for a hard reset. The guitars and dark folk traces that once framed the project have been pushed aside in favor of body music, synth-pop, and machine-driven club pressure. New Order’s Technique, Nitzer Ebb’s Belief, Psychic TV’s Towards Thee Infinite Beat, and Anne Clark’s Pressure Points hover nearby as useful coordinates, although Rowell keeps the material personal enough to avoid sounding like a man trapped beneath a collapsing record collection. Crush Of Souls’ rhythms move with the blunt authority of warehouse machinery, while the drums crack with enough force to make your landlord inspect the ceiling. These rhythms give Rowell room to write about politics, sex, labor, family, and youth as a vanishing resource. His voice carries the exhaustion of somebody who has crossed too many borders and still has enough nerve to flirt at customs. Romance remains present, though it usually appears with a split lip and questionable identification. Across the record, desire keeps colliding with bureaucracy, mortality, and the sort of private ruin no nightclub stamp can excuse. Dying To Stay Young cuts deep. Its family has been starved of affection, surrounded by violence, and taught to regard survival as another form of punishment. Blades, prisons, fire, graves, and fallen angels crowd the lyric, while youth becomes a condition everyone is desperate to preserve even as the body and the world conspire against it. The repeated appeal for the sun to open wide gives the song a strange grandeur, as though daylight itself might expose the damage or burn away whatever remains. Joshua Hourigan’s video extends that unease through snowbound landscapes, fractured edits, spectral figures, and an old castle that looks overdue for either an exorcism or Enya and her army of cats. A spirit dancer appears behind windows, veiled and confined, their movements suggesting souls held inside a structure that has forgotten why it keeps them. Glitches interrupt the scenery, turning the surrounding wilderness into a damaged transmission from somewhere colder and less forgiving. Watch the video for Dying to Stay Young below: Captive Youth is lean, physical, and politically alert, carrying Rowell’s wandering-worker sensibility into a tougher electronic frame. The album understands that staying young can become another exhausting job, complete with bad hours, no benefits, and a manager named Death, who never approves leave. Captive Youth is out now via Avant! Records. Order and stream the album here. items.excerpt: On Old Mill, the penultimate track from Chalk Teeth’s self-titled debut, the Los Angeles trio turns repetition into an engine of dread. items.body: On Old Mill, the penultimate track from Chalk Teeth’s self-titled debut, the Los Angeles trio turns repetition into an engine of dread. Chalk Teeth’s geographical history – Los Angeles by way of New York City and Oakland – feels audible in the song’s mixture of downtown abrasion, warehouse discipline, and West Coast scale. Karolina’s eerie Polish vocal rises through the mass with a cold clarity, delivering an apocalyptic dream of flaming galleons suspended in the sky. The title began as Miller’s working name for the track, chosen before he understood Karolina’s lyrics. Its images of smoke, spinning metal blades and burning lumber happened to meet her vision midway. The song seems governed by accidental correspondences: disco electronics and noise rock, dream imagery and physical labour, ecstatic movement and looming catastrophe. Those elements collect without becoming cluttered, because the trio understands how to leave a severe melodic line exposed inside the distortion. Her guitar, sharp and glacial, cuts across Wallace’s broader sheets of noise, producing a tension between precision and collapse. Each instrument appears to push against the others, yet the song remains locked to its central motion, advancing with the indifferent certainty of industrial machinery. A drum-machine pattern circles with the severe patience of early electronic body music, while Jason Miller’s bass and sequences establish a hard, metallic floor beneath Adam Wallace’s overdriven guitar. The opening suggests a malevolent cousin to Charanjit Singh’s 12 Ragas to the Disco Beat, rerouted through John Carpenter’s anxious minimalism, before the arrangement swells into a dense collision of fuzz, feedback and blunt rhythmic force. The hypnotic drone also calls to mind the sinister undertones of Lebanon Hanover and the catchiness of Pixies in the curious backbeat. Wallace’s accompanying video extends that logic into a piece of expressionist street theatre. The band hauls a railroad tie through an industrial district, maneuvers black geometric fabric, and breaks into abrupt, awkward dances that recall silent cinema without settling into pastiche. Shot by cinematographer Benjamin Kasulke near the group’s North Hollywood studio, the clip benefits from the blunt texture of its surroundings: concrete, debris, vacant lots and the peculiar civic afterlife of discarded materials. The railroad tie itself was found in the middle of the road after the band failed to source one, an intervention from North Hollywood’s vast informal archive of rubbish. Carried through the frame, it resembles a relic, a burden and a corpse. Chalk Teeth become pallbearers for obsolete American infrastructure, escorting it toward an unknown sentence while Old Mill churns behind them. Watch the video for Old Mill below: Chalk Teeth’s Old Mill is severe, strange, and physically persuasive: dance music for a factory condemned by fire, still operating after everyone has fled. Its violence is controlled, its imagery lucid, and its propulsion strong enough to make catastrophe feel briefly communal, even strangely celebratory, under immense pressure. Chalk Teeth’s self-titled debut album is out now as of June 26th on DNTL Records. Listen to Old Mill below and order the album here. items.body: There are several aspects of Scenes that make me feel nostalgic, starting from the moment I first held the physical edition in my hand. It’s a classic black jewel case CD-R with inserts straight out of the turn of the millennium—everything from the fonts and typography used to the specific shade of blue reminds me of early Troniks or Crionic Mind designs, or even some forgotten shoegaze disc on Projekt. The music itself also evokes a fondly remembered West Coast era, albeit in a decidedly fresh and unique way: this ambitious debut by brand-new local project Lily (Keegan Bonds-Harmon) stands out from the pack with an organic all-analog approach, echoing such classics as Instinct & Emotion and Blind Frenchies and Pork with its quiet mastering and glassy crunch. The two extended recordings (running thirteen and thirty-three minutes) sound like they underwent little to no editing, instead embracing the freeform drift of exploratory rehearsal sessions. “Stinging Air” is an impressive start, steadily growing in intensity as squealing tones twirl and twist around each other, with well-timed effects distorting and eventually shattering them into crystalline shards. The heavy use of mixer feedback makes Scenes right at home on the Robert Fuchs roster, but what sets this material apart is its psychedelic spaciousness; even at moments when there’s a lot going on, there’s still so much room to spare. Much of “Dreams Collide” is quite sparse, with a few almost noodly bits that strip the action down to the simple turning of a knob or two—and even what sounds like some FM radio scrubbing—before the track follows through on its title and an icy hell breaks loose. This is noise that deserves rapt attention on a good stereo or set of headphones. Each listen has me eager for another. Bonds-Harmon has a clear vision on his first release that many artists are still searching for on their tenth. Copies are available from the label via email: robert.c.fuchs@gmail.com.

items.body: Analfabetism Konsten Att Andas Med En Grep Genom Ena Lungan Fluttering Dragon Records A dozen or so years into the project’s lifespan, it feels safe to now call Analfabetism the primary project of Fredrik Djurfeldt, the Swedish producer tied to at least ten projects running the EBM to death industrial gamut, active and otherwise. Rooted specifically in that latter genre and its storied history in Sweden, Analfabetism has come to feel like the most fully fleshed out and developed entity yet concocted by Djurfeldt, certainly thanks in part due to his relocation to the country’s desolate and rural north. New LPKonsten Att Andas Med En Grep Genom Ena Lungan, the tenth by our count, both circles back to the core sounds and themes which have been such a reliable wellspring for Djurfeldt, while also pushing a few of Analfebetism’s implicit boundaries. While still holding to an unyielding aesthetic – cold, barren, and distorted – more than any Analfabetism release in recent memory, Konsten Att Andas changes its pitch up by offsetting pure blasts of death industrial styled noise with some of the smoothest and most abstract elements of dark ambient that Djurfeldt has ever drawn upon. While previous releases might have worked to connote wintry desolation with dusty and speckled field ambience, the deep and clean shifting pads of “Den andra feberdrömmen” feel wholly removed from both landscapes and the human perspective itself. Similarly, It seems odd to describe the metallic scrapes and resonances which begin to echo through the middle section of “Den ena feberdrömmen” as “delicate”, but here we are. The art and craft of how those sounds communicate menace alongside a sense of compositional richness (and even, god forbid, tonality) speaks to just how comfortable Djurfeldt now is within the project’s remit. Of course, these variances don’t mark a total shift in Analfabetism – the abyssal drones and tremoring hums of closer “Den blostertid nu fan aldrig kommer” are more representative of the earthier read on dark ambient we’ve come to expect from the project. The same goes for the digitally crushed and backmasked vocal samples which are effectively the only lexical firmpoint of the record, apart from cryptic titles which perhaps draw upon both folklore and subsistence farming. Death industrial’s not for everyone, and the sheer amount of depressive yet intense fare in which one has to immerse oneself in order to ferret out the particulars of specific releases itself makes for a challenge. But for aficionados of the bleak, Analfabetism’s entering into a masterful phase, with Djurfeldt flexing considerable creative muscle. Buy it. items.body: Ambient and Berlin School electronic duo Cells Interlinked, based in Lviv, Ukraine, release the digital album Cold Spring Notes on Cyclical Dreams. The album went online on May 22, 2026, and runs across six tracks: “Water Wheel,” “Cloudy Lake & Little Fishes,” “I’m SQ: Stream,” “I’m SQ: Flow,” “Cold Spring Day,” and “Drift (Summer Memories About Spring).” ‘Cold Spring Notes’ mixes Berlin School sequencing with field recordings “Cold Spring Notes” combines Berlin School-style analogue sequencing with ambient electronics, field recordings and live analogue synth improvisation. Rather than addressing the war directly, the duo describes the record as centered on attentive listening and shifts in perception experienced while living and creating in Ukraine during wartime. Setting out that intent, Cells Interlinked “reflects on attentive listening and the subtle transformations of perception” that emerged from that period. Cold Spring Notes by Cells Interlinked Cyclical Dreams has previously issued releases covered by Side-Line, including D*Time’s “Nightwoven” and Christian Wittman’s “Andromeda”, both also positioned within the ambient and Berlin School space. About Cells Interlinked Cells Interlinked is an ambient, Berlin School and experimental electronic project based in Lviv, Ukraine, formed by Albert and Maria Zakharov. Both musicians have released electronic, industrial, EDM and indie-rock music for more than twenty years before combining forces in this project. Their sound draws on analogue synthesizers, guitar, acoustic instruments and vocals, sometimes processed through a vocoder, with stated reference points including Klaus Schulze, Tangerine Dream’s Virgin-era work, Vince Clarke and Brian Eno. Cells Interlinked released the album “Within” on February 28, 2025, through the label Sincronía del Viento. That record is rooted in ambient and traditional electronic music but includes darker, post-industrial and experimental pieces, among them the tracks “Within,” “Eternity,” “Nightfall” and “Constructions Dissolve.” “Cold Spring Notes” follows “Within” as the duo’s next full release, moving to Cyclical Dreams for its Berlin School-centered sequel.

items.body: Ukrainian ambient artist Bohdan Stupak releases the eight-track album “a place in memories” on Projekt Records on August 7, 2026. The album is available as a name-your-price digital download on Bandcamp and is Stupak’s twelfth release overall, and his second for the Philadelphia-based label, following “book of sorrow” in October 2025. a place in memories by Bohdan Stupak “a place in memories” moves through eight tracks: “endless fields,” “horizon,” “orchards,” “mist,” “old porch,” “whispers,” “rings on the water” and “fireflies.” The genres span ambient, drone, minimalism and dark ambient. The concept behind ‘a place in memories’ Stupak traces the album’s origin to a memory of the Black Sea from 2017, a part of Ukraine now under occupation. He explained the idea in the album’s release notes: “Initially, the idea for this album came to me while recalling good times I had in 2017 at the Black Sea. I caught myself thinking that I consider this (now occupied) part of Ukraine not as a geographic region but rather as a certain point in the past. A time when I was full of hope, love, and the future seemed like a straight, easy stride. I think many of us have a certain place where they felt that way. A place in memories.” “So I decided to expand this concept. Musically, the album has two voices: one of them is a low, massive, mostly major drone, the other one is a collection of various high-pitched drones of different feelings and textures. Some of them are slightly dissonant, others are passionate, some are minor. This is how memory plays tricks on us: making some things better upon reflection than they actually were back then or presenting some good things as bittersweet because they have passed.” “Through the course of the album, music gets darker and more tense, yet at some point things break and new abstract textures arrive: computer-generated bells, crackles, plucks. This is how bravely facing the dark corners of our past enriches our personalities with new facets.” “This is how the album ends: with soothing closure, a combination of various textures and methods.” About Bohdan Stupak Bohdan Stupak is an ambient and drone artist based in Kyiv, Ukraine, who mixes minimalist and experimental electronic music. His tenth release, “book of sorrow,” came out on Projekt Records on October 3, 2025: a six-track work built from a single processed guitar, sitting between ambient and neoclassical music. “a place in memories,” his twelfth release, is his second album for the label, continuing that relationship. Stupak’s catalog spans several other labels and self-releases on Bandcamp; no independent Discogs entry for the artist is available to cross-check the full chronology. Projekt Records, based in Philadelphia, US, has released and reissued material from acts including Black Tape For A Blue Girl, Lycia, VEiiLA, Unto Ashes and Stratosphere.

items.body: A Certain Ratio, the Manchester post-punk and funk group, have shared a new mix of “Tumba Rumba”, built from the original session tapes by Andy Meecham of The Emperor Machine. The track appears on The Joy of Sextet, one of two anniversary companion albums the band releases on Mute on 28 August 2026. “Tumba Rumba” originally appeared as the b-side of the 1982 Factory 7″ single “Knife Slits Water” (FAC 62). A Certain Ratio described the mix in a statement: “We are immensely proud of this song and Andy has done a great job of bringing it sonically into 2026. If it doesn’t move your feet, and expand your mind, you need to give your head a wobble.” ‘The Joy of Sextet’ and ‘Force Majeure’ companion albums A Certain Ratio mark two anniversaries in 2026: 45 years since recording “Sextet” at Revolution Studios in Cheadle Hulme, Stockport, and 40 years since the release of “Force”. “The Joy of Sextet” is a nine-track companion to the 1982 album, newly mixed by Meecham from the original 1981 two-inch multitrack tapes and featuring “Tumba Rumba”, “Knife Slits Water”, “Lucinda”, “Crystal”, “Gum”, “Day One”, “Below the Canal” and “Waterline”. The second companion, “Force Majeure”, reworks the 1986 album “Force” and adds previously unreleased versions produced by the band with the late Stuart James, including the title track “Force” that was left off the original. Both arrive on 28 August 2026 on limited coloured vinyl – “The Joy of Curacao” for “The Joy of Sextet” and “Unforced Purple” for “Force Majeure” – plus CD and digital formats. Side-Line reported on the two companion albums and their announcement in an earlier article, and the band previously worked with Meecham on his reworking of “Constant Curve” in 2023. A Certain Ratio – Jez Kerr, Donald Johnson, Martin Moscrop and Martha “Tilly” Tilson – tour the UK in October 2026 to mark the two anniversaries, playing both albums in full; the full run of dates is listed in Side-Line’s report on “Knife Slits Water”. About A Certain Ratio A Certain Ratio formed in Greater Manchester in 1977, initially as a duo of vocalist Simon Topping and guitarist Peter Terrell, soon joined by bassist and vocalist Jez Kerr, guitarist and trumpeter Martin Moscrop, drummer Donald Johnson and vocalist Martha “Tilly” Tilson. The band debuted on Tony Wilson’s Factory Records in September 1979 with “All Night Party”, produced by Martin Hannett, and released the cassette-only “The Graveyard and the Ballroom” in January 1980. Early singles “Flight” and “Waterline” reached the UK Independent Chart top ten, and the band’s debut studio album, “To Each…”, topped the Independent Chart in May 1981. “Sextet”, A Certain Ratio’s self-produced third album, followed in January 1982, drawing on the acid jazz, funk and Latin influences the band had picked up in New York; it topped the indie albums chart and reached number 55 on the UK Albums Chart. The 1982 single “Knife Slits Water” carried “Tumba Rumba” as its b-side. After Topping and Terrell left in late 1982, the group continued as Kerr, Moscrop and Johnson, releasing “Force” in November 1986, co-produced with Stuart James, which reached number two on the UK Independent Albums Chart and was the band’s last album for Factory. A Certain Ratio subsequently recorded for A&M Records (1989-90), Rob’s Records (1991-92) and other independent labels, with reissues on Creation’s Rev-Ola imprint and Soul Jazz Records. In 2018, Mute Records began reissuing the band’s catalogue, starting with “acr:set”, followed by the 40th-anniversary box set “acr:box” in 2019. “ACR Loco” (2020) was the band’s first album of new material in twelve years, followed by “1982” (2023) and “It All Comes Down to This” (2024). “The Joy of Sextet” and “Force Majeure”, carrying the new “Tumba Rumba” mix, extend that Mute partnership into the 45th and 40th anniversaries of “Sextet” and “Force”.

items.body: Rochdale Music Stories will release the compilation “Kenion Street” on August 7 via Alcopop Records, on limited-edition orange vinyl and digital platforms. The album gathers emerging Rochdale artists reinterpreting tracks originally recorded at the city’s Cargo Studios and Suite 16 studios, both located on Kenion Street, between 1977 and 2001. The project comes from a collaboration between the Stockport Music Story, Voltalab Sound Studios and Alcopop Records, funded by Arts Council England, Rochdale Development Agency and Rochdale Borough Council, as part of Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester’s Town of Culture. The eleven tracks were recorded and produced by Jamie Alsop at Voltalab Sound Studios. Two tracks were made available ahead of the release: Desyfer and Emma Konnanov’s electro rework of Happy Mondays’ “Twenty Four Hour Party People,” and K-Estate’s synth-pop reinterpretation of Gang of Four’s “Damaged Goods.” Discussing the album, Alcopop Records’ Jack Clothier stated the label was “linking up with our good friends at Rough Trade to bring Rochdale Hour to London, Bristol, Nottingham and Liverpool,” inviting fans “to come listen to our first Rochdale Music Stories album, Kenion Street.” The full tracklist covers acts including Joy Division, Gang Of Four, Happy Mondays, Inspiral Carpets, The Chameleons, OMD, New Order, A Certain Ratio, Nico, The Fall and Stone Roses: Micah Stalgic ft. Local Vocals – “Atmosphere” (Joy Division) K-Estate – “Damaged Goods” (Gang of Four) Desyfer & Emma Konnanov – “Twenty Four Hour Party People” (Happy Mondays) P*STARR – “Keep The Circle Around” (Inspiral Carpets) Leo HC – “Up The Down Escalator” (The Chameleons) PoolEra – “Electricity” (OMD) Medley – “Dreams Never End” (New Order) Blvckout – “All Night Party” (A Certain Ratio) The Velvet Shadow ft. Maisie Thompson – “All Tomorrow’s Parties” (Nico) Jennifer Reid – “Totally Wired” (The Fall) From The Ground Up ft. Bloom Music Community – “Elephant Stone” (The Stone Roses) Free launch listening parties, billed as “Rochdale Hour,” take place August 8 at 3pm at Rough Trade shops in London, Bristol, Nottingham and Liverpool, with the full album played and beer from Heywood’s Phoenix Brewery. On August 7, Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, Peter Hook & The Light and A Certain Ratio play a concert in Rochdale marking the album’s release. About Kenion Street and Rochdale Music Stories Between 1977 and 2001, Kenion Street in Rochdale housed both Cargo Studios and its successor, Suite 16, where Joy Division, New Order, OMD, The Stone Roses, The Fall, Happy Mondays, A Certain Ratio and The Chameleons, among others, recorded some of their best-known work. Rochdale Music Stories launched in 2026 to mark Rochdale’s year as Greater Manchester’s Town of Culture, pairing emerging local artists with the studios’ recorded legacy through Voltalab Sound Studios, built on the former Cargo site. The “Kenion Street” compilation is the project’s first album release, following a live launch concert at Heywood Civic in March 2026 where the participating artists performed their reinterpretations.

items.body: German EBM/synthpop project ES23, the solo outlet of Daniel Pad, released the new single Fairytale via Infacted Recordings on July 31, 2026. The track is available as a digital download and stream. “Fairytale” is a purely instrumental piece that runs 3:58. On his own website, Daniel Pad describes it as a playful musical journey where driving psytrance elements meet epic, gentle strings, adding that the track carries detailed rhythmic work and subtle gaming-related references in its sound design, giving the piece both a nostalgic and futuristic character. The single is tagged EBM, industrial, synthpop, futurepop, electro and melodic techno on Bandcamp. On Bandcamp the release itself is titled “Fairytales”, the same one-track digital release carrying the song “Fairytale”. Fairytale by ES23 About ES23 ES23 is the solo project of German producer Daniel Patschkowski, known as Daniel Pad, founded in Bochum, Germany at the end of 2004. The project released its first official album, “Heaven Or Hell”, in 2012 through Infacted Recordings, followed by “Mutatio Ex Machina” in 2014. Side-Line reviewed the third album, “Erase My Heart”, in July 2017, describing it as a merge of dark-electro, EBM and future-pop, and featured Daniel Pad in a “Click Interview” the following month. The fourth album, “Only Melodies Remain”, followed in December 2020, mixing Electro-Pop with harder EBM elements and featuring a collaboration with SynthAttack plus remixes by Solitary Experiments and Shiv-R. Side-Line spoke with Daniel Pad again in a “Click Interview” in January 2021, where he stated “I’m not a huge fan producing the same music over and over again. I need variation.” The fifth album, “Dancing With Clouds”, arrived in November 2023, again through Infacted Recordings. With “Fairytale”, ES23 continues that release history in 2026 with a purely instrumental single on the same label.

items.body: Norwegian electronic rock artist Mortiis has released “Farewell Romero,” the fourth and final single from his album “Ghosts Of Europa” (Prophecy Productions, released June 26, 2026). The single is now available on all major streaming platforms and concludes the album’s single campaign, following earlier singles including the title track and “Violent Silence.” “Farewell Romero” arrives alongside two exclusive bonus tracks. “Violent Silence (Madrigal Version)” features vocalist Laurie Ann Haus, known as the frontwoman of Todesbonden and for her session work on Blizzard game soundtracks, and was mixed by Sean Beavan, who also mixed the “Ghosts Of Europa” album. The second bonus track is an alternative version of “Farewell Romero” featuring French pianist Nicolas Horvath, mixed by Marc Urselli. In the announcement accompanying the release, Mortiis described “Farewell Romero” as a strong contender for his favourite of the four singles from “Ghosts Of Europa.” He also shared a new series of photographs taken by his wife, Linda Ellefsen, showing their daughter Enya Ellefsen holding various vinyl editions of the album. According to Mortiis, the photos were taken at the same location used for the “Ghosts Of Europa” artwork. Tour dates for Mortiis after ‘Farewell Romero’ The release comes just ahead of an extensive international tour that will take Mortiis across Latin America, Oceania and Japan. October 2026 – Oct. 7 – Mexico City, Mexico – Circo Volador – Oct. 8 – Guadalajara, Mexico – Foro Independencia – Oct. 9 – Chihuahua, Mexico – Pistoleros – Oct. 10 – Tijuana, Mexico – Dragon Rojo Bar – Oct. 11 – Monterrey, Mexico – Café Iguana – Oct. 14 – Bogotá, Colombia – Ace of Spades – Oct. 16 – São Paulo, Brazil – La Iglesia – Oct. 17 – Buenos Aires, Argentina – Bula – Oct. 18 – Santiago, Chile – Sala RBX November 2026 – Nov. 13 – Auckland, New Zealand – Double Whammy – Nov. 14 – Wellington, New Zealand – Valhalla – Nov. 19 – Marrickville, Australia – Nov. 20 – Brisbane, Australia – Nov. 21 – Thornbury, Australia – Nov. 22 – Adelaide, Australia April 2027 – Apr. 9 – Osaka, Japan – Never Surrender / Hospital Fest Vol. II About Mortiis Mortiis is the project of Norwegian musician Håvard Ellefsen, based in Fredrikstad, Norway. Ellefsen played bass in the black metal band Emperor between 1991 and 1992, contributing to early demos and the 1993 mini-LP, before starting Mortiis as a solo project in 1993. The project’s first phase, later grouped as “Era I,” produced six synthesizer-only albums, including “Født til å Herske” (1993), “Ånden som Gjorde Opprør” (1994), “Keiser Av En Dimensjon Ukjent” (1995) and “Crypt of the Wizard” (1996), now cited as a foundational influence on the dungeon synth genre. Ellefsen took on lead vocals for the first time on “The Smell of Rain” (2001), moving the project into dark wave and electropop, before “The Grudge” (2004) shifted Mortiis into industrial rock. Further albums followed, including “Some Kind of Heroin” (2007) and “Perfectly Defect” (2010). After a break, Mortiis returned with “The Great Deceiver” (2016) and “The Unraveling Mind” (2017), followed in 2020 by “Spirit of Rebellion,” a reworking of “Ånden som Gjorde Opprør.” “Ghosts Of Europa,” recorded between 2020 and 2026, is Mortiis’ first album for Prophecy Productions. Side-Line first reported the release in seven confirmed formats in March 2026, then detailed the full tracklist, guest credits and Australian tour dates closer to the album’s June 26 release. The album developed in part from a planned collaboration between Mortiis and Stephan Groth of Apoptygma Berzerk, who went on to co-produce early vocal recordings. Sean Beavan mixed the album, and it was mastered by Jules Seifert. With “Farewell Romero,” Mortiis closes out the “Ghosts Of Europa” single campaign ahead of his upcoming tour of Latin America, Oceania and Japan.

items.body: After releasing their previous two albums on Icy Cold Records, the American band Darkswoon returns with their latest full-length release, a ten-track album that further explores their signature sound. The band remains faithful to its established influences, balancing between Dark-Wave and Shoegaze while occasionally incorporating elements of Ballads and Dream-Pop. At times, these different styles merge within a single track, beginning with fragile, atmospheric passages before gradually building towards heavier climaxes where the guitars take center stage. Vocalist Jana Cushman’s voice combines sweetness with intensity, delivering performances that are both passionate and emotionally charged. With “Antivenom”, Darkswoon finally manages to fully convince me. The production feels richer and more dynamic, while the album carries a sense of urgency and drive that I had not always detected in their previous work. “Antivenom” is an enjoyable and diverse release that should appeal to listeners with a taste for dark, atmospheric music. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Thread”: Antivenom by Darkswoon About Darkswoon Darkswoon is a band from Portland, Oregon, described on Discogs as playing elektrohaze, a self-styled blend that mixes Dark-Wave and Shoegaze with Ballads and Dream-Pop. The lineup includes Jana Cushman on vocals and guitar, Rachel Ellis on synths and drum machines, Norah Lynn on bass, and Andrew Michael Potter. The band released the album “BIND” on February 9, 2019, followed by “Bloom Decay” on September 14, 2022. Additional Bandcamp releases include the “Eaten By Wolves” EP, the remix collection “Human Faults Remixed”, and the earlier titles “Silhouettes” and “Year One”. Side-Line first covered the band on April 3, 2026, when Darkswoon shared “Antivenom” as the second single from the new album. “Antivenom” was released April 3, 2026 through Viasonde, with the album recorded and produced by Jana Cushman and Jeremy Wilkins and mixed by Jeremy Wilkins.

items.body: Over the last few years, metal of all sub-genres has been doing something that I really love: rediscovering the joy of heavy metal. Now, this is a separate phenomenon than the heavy metal/traditional metal revival. This is not bands making heavy metal per se, but rather making death, black, thrash, progressive and more styles of metal that use heavy metal as their palette. Case in point: Hollowborn. These Florida based hellions are finally answering the question: "what if Morbid Angel had listened to way more Iron Maiden?" The cool thing is that What the Land Reclaims, the project's debut, goes much further than "just" that schtick; it's an album full of great death metal, heavy metal influences aside. But then you add galloping riffs, flamboyant solos, and an overall fantastic tinge to it, and you've got a truly outstanding release.Considering the diversity I mentioned above, I could point you towards many points in the album. If you just hit play, you'll find the opening trio of tracks to be really good death metal. But if you do the opposite and flip on over to "March of Eothas I: Souls of Caed Nua" (oh yeah, this album is also Pillars of Eternity inspired) you'll get a taste of the true beauty of this album. The track opens with this beautiful galloping riff with powerful and evocative chords that would not be out of place on a Fellowship album (high praise indeed). But then there's a classic death metal ough and the track explodes into an absolute shred of a riff. Later on, the heavy metal returns in the form of many (no, I said many) melodic solos which build on the initial energies of the track and allow them to unfurl into a true celebration of metal's might.As I mentioned, there is a lot more on this album. But for me, that love and passion for heavy metal immediately won me over. Listen, it really doesn't matter how may years pass from the first time I heard Killers or how many times I've sung "Painkiller" at a bar or how many nights I've spent burning away the midnight oil by playing Somewhere Far Beyond on repeat. Heavy/power metal will still always be my first flame and the thing which moves my the heart most. And when you take that passion and you marry it with the other (excellent, beloved, amazing) styles of metal that have come forth since metal's beacon was first lit, you get something truly special. That's what Hollowborn's When the Land Reclaims is: a true joy for any fan of heavy metal.Heavy metal will never die! What the Land Reclaims by Hollowborn

半世紀以上におよ... 詳しく見る ※本記事はポッドキャスト番組『ONTOMO Radio』で語られた内容を再構成しています。 『長岡鉄男の仕事 伝説のオーディオ評論家 その生涯とマスターピース』 長岡鉄男 著 2026年7月 音楽之友社 1. 焼肉店でも原稿を書き続けた 取材が終わると、編集者たちと焼肉店へ。普通なら仕事を終えて食事を楽しむ時間ですが、長岡鉄男は違いました。 テーブルに座ると、おもむろに万年筆を取り出し、その場で原稿を書き始めるのです。 焼肉を食べながら、雑談にも加わりながら、それでも手は止まりません。編集者が食事を終える頃には、ベストバイコンポの記事など数本分の原稿がすでに完成。「はい」と手渡された編集者は、そのまま持ち帰ったといいます。 さらに驚くのは、その執筆スタイルでした。途中で考え込んだり、何度も書き直したりすることはほとんどなく、冒頭から最後まで一気に書き進める“一筆書き”。文字数が少しオーバーしたときだけ、「ここをカット」と印を付ける程度で、ほぼ完成原稿になっていたそうです。 「Stereo」元編集部の田中基裕は、「原稿を書いているというより、こんこんと湧き出る言葉を写し取っているようだった」と振り返ります。その圧倒的な仕事の速さは、編集部でも語り草になっていました。 2. スピーカー設計図を600本以上も描いた 長岡鉄男といえば、自作スピーカー。その設計図は、生涯で600本以上にのぼるといわれています。しかも、その1枚1枚が驚くほど緻密です。 代表作であるバックロードホーンは、内部を音の通り道が何度も折れ曲がる複雑な構造。しかし長岡は、その迷路のような内部設計を、まるで製図の見本のように美しい手書きの図面へと描き起こしていました。 編集者がさらに驚いたのは、図面にもほとんど書き直しの跡がなく、迷いなく描き進めて完成させていたこと。原稿と同じように、設計図まで”一筆書き”だったのです。 「この人の頭の中はどうなっているんだろう」。複雑な構造を何種類も考え出し、それを迷いなく図面に落とし込む姿に、編集部の誰もがそう感じていたといいます。 長岡鉄男と代表作「スワン」 3. バブル時代でも「高いものが一番」とは言わなかった 1980〜90年代は、日本のオーディオ黄金期。 高級オーディオが次々と登場し、「高価な機材こそ最高」という空気もありました。 そんな時代に、長岡鉄男が一貫して提案したのは「自作」という選択肢でした。 もちろん高級機も評価します。 しかし、「コストを抑えながら、自分だけの理想の音を追求できる」という自作の価値を最後まで語り続けました。 「平均点の高い音」ではなく、「一点突破の魅力」。 その哲学が、多くのオーディオファンを惹きつけたのです。 4. 毎年7〜8台の新作スピーカーを生み出した 「Stereo」の夏号といえば、自作スピーカーの「工作特集」。読者にとって毎年の恒例企画でしたが、その中心にはいつも長岡鉄男がいました。 驚くのは、その仕事量です。長岡は毎年のように7〜8台もの新作スピーカーを設計。しかも図面を描くだけでは終わりません。編集部が実際にスピーカーを製作して長岡のもとへ運び、丸1日かけて測定や試聴を実施。その結果をもとに誌面へ掲載するという工程を、何十年にもわたって繰り返していました。 1台設計するだけでも大仕事。それを毎年7〜8台も発表し続ける。編集部にとっても、それは夏の一大プロジェクトだったのです。 2000年に長岡が亡くなったとき、「Stereo」編集部で真っ先に話題になったのは「これから工作特集をどうするのか」ということだったといいます。それほどまでに長岡鉄男は、一人の評論家という枠を超え、日本の自作スピーカー文化そのものを支える存在でした。 自作スピーカーと自宅の前で 5. オーディオだけではない！ 文章が抜群に面白かった 今回の書籍制作で、編集者たちが改めて驚いたのがエッセイでした。 政治、歴史、文学、音楽、日常……。どんなテーマでも軽妙に語り、思わず笑ってしまうような文章を書く。 週刊誌連載らしい時代の空気も色濃く残っていて、「今読んでも面白い」という声が編集者の間で相次いだといいます。 オーディオ評論家という肩書だけでは語れない、「書き手」としての魅力もまた、長岡鉄男の大きな才能でした。 6. 評論はたった一言で信頼を勝ち取った オーディオ評論では、スペックや試聴結果など、多くの情報が並びます。そのなかで読者が特に注目していたのが、長岡鉄男が最後に添える短いコメントでした。 必要以上に大げさな表現を使うことはなく、メーカーへの配慮も忘れず、それでも評価すべきものはきちんと評価する。その絶妙な言葉選びが、多くの読者から信頼を集めていたといいます。 長々と褒めるよりも、短い一言のほうが重みを持つ。長岡鉄男の評論には、そんな独特の説得力がありました。 長岡鉄男の究極のホームシアタールーム「方舟」 7. 「未来を思いわずらうより、今を生きる」 『長岡鉄男の仕事 伝説のオーディオ評論家 その生涯とマスターピース』では、最後のページのイラストでこんな言葉をつぶやいています。 未来のことを思いわずらってもしょうがない。現在を精いっぱい生き、仕事をせっせとするのが一番だ。 戦争を経験し、激動の昭和を生きた長岡鉄男。 膨大な原稿を書き、数え切れないほどのスピーカーを設計し、自分が面白いと思うことを追い続けた人生。 その生き方そのものが、多くの人を惹きつけ、「伝説」と呼ばれる理由なのかもしれません。 長岡鉄男の仕事を知ることは、1人のオーディオ評論家を知ることではありません。本書を読み進めるほどに、「伝説」は誇張ではなく、積み重ねられた仕事の量と質が生んだ事実だったことに気づかされます。 『長岡鉄男の仕事 伝説のオーディオ評論家 その生涯とマスターピース』 長岡鉄男 著 2026年7月 音楽之友社 ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら 参加者：宍戸佐弥（MC/書籍課）、田中基裕（書籍課）、吉野俊介（月刊「Stereo」編集長） 月刊「stereo」2026年8月号（方舟の現在とこれから／オーディオ小僧のHi-Fiスクラップブック 長岡鉄男という名の好奇心 他） 長岡鉄男関連の書籍・MOOK ONTOMO Shop オーディオ関連

items.body: There are several aspects of Scenes that make me feel nostalgic, starting from the moment I first held the physical edition in my hand. It’s a classic black jewel case CD-R with inserts straight out of the turn of the millennium—everything from the fonts and typography used to the specific shade of blue reminds me of early Troniks or Crionic Mind designs, or even some forgotten shoegaze disc on Projekt. The music itself also evokes a fondly remembered West Coast era, albeit in a decidedly fresh and unique way: this ambitious debut by brand-new local project Lily (Keegan Bonds-Harmon) stands out from the pack with an organic all-analog approach, echoing such classics as Instinct & Emotion and Blind Frenchies and Pork with its quiet mastering and glassy crunch. The two extended recordings (running thirteen and thirty-three minutes) sound like they underwent little to no editing, instead embracing the freeform drift of exploratory rehearsal sessions. “Stinging Air” is an impressive start, steadily growing in intensity as squealing tones twirl and twist around each other, with well-timed effects distorting and eventually shattering them into crystalline shards. The heavy use of mixer feedback makes Scenes right at home on the Robert Fuchs roster, but what sets this material apart is its psychedelic spaciousness; even at moments when there’s a lot going on, there’s still so much room to spare. Much of “Dreams Collide” is quite sparse, with a few almost noodly bits that strip the action down to the simple turning of a knob or two—and even what sounds like some FM radio scrubbing—before the track follows through on its title and an icy hell breaks loose. This is noise that deserves rapt attention on a good stereo or set of headphones. Each listen has me eager for another. Bonds-Harmon has a clear vision on his first release that many artists are still searching for on their tenth. Copies are available from the label via email: robert.c.fuchs@gmail.com.

items.album: 知的障害・発達障害のある子どもと家族へのアプローチ
items.excerpt: ――程度別の特徴からコミュニケーション方法、特別支援学級の勧め方、就学相談の進め方まではじめに軽度・中度・重度の知的障害、あるいはASD（自閉スペクトラム症）・ADHD（注意欠如多動症）・LD（学習障害）などの発達障害のある子どもとその家族を支えるには、医学的な理解、コミュニケーションの技術、教育制度の知識、そして家族の心理プロセスへの配慮という、複数の視点が同時に必要になります。この記事では、公的機関（文部科学省・厚生労働省・こども家庭庁・内閣府）の資料と、専門機関・現場経験者の発信をもとに、できるだけ幅広く、省かずに情報を整理しました。教員、支援者、そして当事者家族の方の実務・実生活の参考になれば幸いです。■1章 知的障害の程度別の特徴を理解する知的障害は、IQ（知能指数）の目安と日常生活における適応行動の状態の両方から、軽度・中度・重度・最重度に分類されます。ただし数値はあくまで目安であり、一人ひとりの状態は大きく異なる点に注意が必要です。【軽度知的障害（IQおおむね50〜69）】食事・トイレ・着替えなど基本的な生活動作はほぼ自立して行えることが多く、ある程度の年齢まで周囲が障害
items.body: ――程度別の特徴からコミュニケーション方法、特別支援学級の勧め方、就学相談の進め方まではじめに軽度・中度・重度の知的障害、あるいはASD（自閉スペクトラム症）・ADHD（注意欠如多動症）・LD（学習障害）などの発達障害のある子どもとその家族を支えるには、医学的な理解、コミュニケーションの技術、教育制度の知識、そして家族の心理プロセスへの配慮という、複数の視点が同時に必要になります。この記事では、公的機関（文部科学省・厚生労働省・こども家庭庁・内閣府）の資料と、専門機関・現場経験者の発信をもとに、できるだけ幅広く、省かずに情報を整理しました。教員、支援者、そして当事者家族の方の実務・実生活の参考になれば幸いです。■1章 知的障害の程度別の特徴を理解する知的障害は、IQ（知能指数）の目安と日常生活における適応行動の状態の両方から、軽度・中度・重度・最重度に分類されます。ただし数値はあくまで目安であり、一人ひとりの状態は大きく異なる点に注意が必要です。【軽度知的障害（IQおおむね50〜69）】食事・トイレ・着替えなど基本的な生活動作はほぼ自立して行えることが多く、ある程度の年齢まで周囲が障害に気づかないケースもあります。読み書き計算や抽象的思考など特定の学習技能の習得に難しさが出やすく、対人コミュニケーションやスケジュール管理を苦手とすることがあります。適切な時間をかけた指導によって、家事や身の回りのことをかなりの部分自分でこなせるようになる場合もあります。参考：https://visit.aiai-cc.co.jp/column/mild-intellectual-disability-guide/参考：https://junior.litalico.jp/column/article/095/【中度知的障害（IQおおむね35〜49）】一部の生活動作は自立して行えても、全てを一人でこなすにはサポートが必要になることが多い段階です。ひらがなでの読み書きや簡単な会話はできますが、判断力や意思決定には時間がかかります。買い物や交通機関の利用なども、繰り返しの練習と周囲の支援があれば少しずつできることが増えていきます。参考：https://www.ajscrum.co.jp/business/job-assistance/column/moderate-intellectual-disability-support/参考：https://works.manaby.co.jp/column/29210/【重度・最重度知的障害】食事・着替え・入浴など、日常生活の多くの場面で日々のサポートが必要です。重度の場合、2歳ごろまでに運動・言語・対人コミュニケーションの面で遅れがみられ、早期に診断がつくこともあります。学習技能の習得は初等教育段階程度にとどまることが多く、コミュニケーションや意思決定には周囲の継続的な支援が欠かせません。参考：https://junior.litalico.jp/column/article/095/参考：https://junior.litalico.jp/column/article/101/【知的障害と発達障害の関係】DSM-5では知的障害（知的発達症）は発達障害（神経発達症群）のカテゴリーに含まれています。知的障害は18歳未満の発達期に現れますが、ASDやADHDなどの発達障害の特性が重なって現れることも少なくありません。「軽度知的障害だと思っていたら実はASDの特性による困りごとだった」というケースもあるため、専門機関での丁寧なアセスメントが重要です。参考：https://www.welbe.co.jp/campus/case/intellectual_disability.html■2章 発達障害（ASD・ADHD・LD・DCD）の種類と特徴発達障害は単独で現れるというより、複数の特性が重なり合って現れることが多いのが特徴です。【ASD（自閉スペクトラム症）】対人関係の読み取りの難しさ、強いこだわり、感覚の過敏・鈍麻などが特徴です。相手の表情や場の空気を読むことが苦手だったり、興味のあることを一方的に話してしまったり、特定の音に過敏に反応したりする様子がみられることがあります。かつて「アスペルガー症候群」と呼ばれていた特性も、現在はASDに含めて説明されるのが一般的です。参考：https://yobouiryoukai.com/developmental-disorders-types/【ADHD（注意欠如多動症）】「不注意」（忘れ物が多い、集中が続かない）「多動性」（じっとしていられない）「衝動性」（順番を待てない、考える前に行動する）が主な特性です。多動の傾向は幼児期から小学生ごろに目立ちやすく、成長とともに変化していくこともあります。参考：https://hugkum.sho.jp/62831【LD／SLD（学習障害・限局性学習症）】全般的な知的発達に遅れはないものの、読む・書く・計算するなど特定の分野の習得に強い難しさが出る状態です。「努力不足」「怠けている」と誤解されやすい点が大きな課題であり、周囲の正しい理解が欠かせません。参考：https://yobouiryoukai.com/developmental-disorders-types/【DCD（発達性協調運動症）】運動面の不器用さが目立つ特性で、ASDやADHDと同じグループに位置づけられることがありますが、認知度が低く「運動神経が悪いだけ」と見過ごされがちです。参考：https://hikosan-blog.com/hattatsu-shougai-shurui-chigai/いずれの特性も「育て方の問題」ではなく生まれつきの脳の特性であり、早期に気づいて適切な支援につなげることで、本人の生きやすさが大きく変わるとされています。■3章 子どもへの関わり方・アプローチの基本程度や特性ごとの違いはあっても、共通して大切にされている関わり方の考え方があります。・できないことを叱るより、できたことを具体的に、その場で伝える・指示は一度に一つずつ、短く具体的な言葉で伝える・見通しが持てるように、その日の予定や活動の順序を事前に伝える・「気持ちを察する」ことを過度に期待せず、言葉や視覚情報で明確に伝える・環境の刺激（音・光・人の多さ）を調整し、落ち着ける場を用意する・成功体験を積み重ね、自己肯定感を育てることを優先するASDのある子どもとの接し方では、人との関わりが少なくて済む環境を整えたり、暗黙の了解を前提とせず具体的に伝えたりすることがポイントとして挙げられています。参考：https://sanyokai-clinic.com/kokoro/6172/■4章 コミュニケーション方法（視覚支援・TEACCH・PECS・AAC）言葉だけに頼らないコミュニケーション支援の方法は、知的障害・発達障害のある子どもの生活の質を大きく左右します。【視覚的スケジュール・構造化（TEACCHプログラム）】1980年代に米国ノースカロライナ大学で始まったTEACCHプログラムは、「物理的構造化」「スケジュール」「ワークシステム」「視覚的構造化」という4つの手法で、自閉症の子どもたちの学習や生活を支える考え方です。自閉症の子どもは音声情報より視覚情報を記憶しやすい傾向があるとされ、一日の流れをカードや表で示す視覚的スケジュールは、見通しを持たせ、行動の切り替えをスムーズにする効果があるとされています。特性を「自閉症の文化」として肯定的に捉え、強みを活かす支援の考え方も特徴です。参考：https://h-navi.jp/column/article/650参考：https://theprompt.jp/schedules/【PECS（絵カード交換式コミュニケーションシステム）】1985年に米国で開発された、絵カードを用いた拡大・代替コミュニケーション（AAC）の方法です。自発的なコミュニケーションを身につけることを目的としており、教師・施設職員・家族でも比較的簡単に導入できる点が特徴です。早期から使用することで発語につながったケースも報告されています。参考：https://h-navi.jp/column/article/731【AAC（拡大・代替コミュニケーション）全般】話し言葉によるコミュニケーションに困難がある子どもに向けて、絵カードや文字盤、タブレット端末の音声出力アプリなど、様々な手段でコミュニケーションを補う考え方の総称です。最初から相手に手渡す・提示するという「伝える」体験を作れる点が、信頼関係の構築にもつながるとされています。■5章 家族へのアプローチ――保護者の心理プロセスを理解する【障害受容の4段階モデル】家族支援の現場では、保護者が子どもの障害を受け止めていく過程として「ショック→否認→怒り・絶望→再起・適応」という四段階のモデルが定説として知られています。この順序には一定の傾向がある一方、どれくらいの時間で通過するかに基準はなく、数か月で進む人もいれば、十数年かけても完全には通過しきれない場合もあります。また受容は一方向的なものではなく、一度は適応段階に達したように見えても、何かのきっかけで否認やショックの段階に戻ることもあると指摘されています。参考：https://www.dinf.ne.jp/doc/japanese/prdl/jsrd/norma/n312/n312003.html参考：https://plusinnovation.jp/blogdetail?wgd=blog-130&wgdo=date-DESC%2Csort-ASC支援者が子どもの発達支援を行うことは、そのまま家族支援につながります。ただし支援者と家族の間で「子どもにどう育ってほしいか」という方向性にズレが生じることもあるため、家族のライフサイクルや発達過程への理解を持って、意図的に橋渡しをすることが大切だとされています。また、子ども本人の障害受容のペースと、保護者の受容のペースがずれることにも注意が必要です。本人が特性を受け入れ始めている一方で、保護者が「まだ治るかもしれない」と考えている場合、支援の方向性に齟齬が生まれることがあるため、当事者へのアプローチと家族へのアプローチは、別々に、しかし連携しながら進める必要があるとされています。【ペアレントトレーニング・ペアレントプログラム】保護者が子どもの行動を観察して特性を理解し、ほめ方・しかり方・指示の出し方・環境調整の仕方などを学ぶことで、子どもの困った行動の減少や、家族自身の養育不安・抑うつの軽減を目指す取り組みです。応用行動分析（ABA）をベースにしたプログラムなど複数の種類があり、6〜8回程度のセッションを通じて講義とワーク、ホームワークの共有を繰り返すのが一般的な形式です。目的は子育てのテクニック習得だけでなく、子育て仲間づくりや、親子で子育てを楽しめるようになることも含まれています。参考：https://h-navi.jp/column/article/766参考：https://www.rehab.go.jp/ddis/howto/parents/【子ども本人への障害の伝え方（告知）】「いつ、どのように伝えるか」は多くの保護者が悩むテーマです。ポジティブな情報はできる限り具体的に伝える、本人が理解できる言葉を選ぶ、といった点がポイントとして挙げられています。告知の方法や時期は家庭によって様々であり、正解が一つに決まっているわけではありません。参考：https://famicare.jp/2025/10/01/how-to-communicate-disability-diagnosis-to-child/参考：https://sole.education/labo/all-ages/disability-announcement/【学校（担任・特別支援教育コーディネーター）への伝え方】学校への情報共有の手段としては、連絡帳や連絡アプリ、面談などがあります。継続的なサポートや進路・所属学級に関わる相談など、内容が重い場合は、担任だけでなく、各校に配置されている特別支援教育コーディネーターに相談することも勧められています。「何を、どこまで伝えるか」は、子どもの個性や気持ち、家庭の考え方、将来の展望などをふまえて個別に判断することが大切だとされています。子どもの特性・関わり方・支援方法・利用してきたサポート機関などをまとめて記入する「サポートブック」を活用すると、担任以外の関係者（スクールカウンセラーなど）とも情報を共有しやすくなります。自治体の福祉窓口やウェブサイトで配布されていることが多く、確認しておくとよいでしょう。参考：https://tokyo-yagaku.jp/column/dd-ht-inform/参考：https://www.rakurakumom.com/single-post/team-support■6章 特別支援教育の仕組み――通常学級・通級・特別支援学級・特別支援学校の違い障害のある子どもの学びの場は、大きく分けて次の4種類があります。・通常学級：通常のクラスに在籍し、必要に応じて合理的配慮を受けながら学ぶ・通級指導教室（通級）：通常学級に在籍しながら、週数回程度、別の教室で特別な指導を受ける。比較的軽度な障害が対象で、小学校・中学校・高等学校に設置されている・特別支援学級（支援級）：小学校・中学校に設置される少人数制（原則1クラス8名定員）のクラス。障害種別ごとに学級が分かれており、対象は知的障害、肢体不自由、病弱・身体虚弱、弱視、難聴、言語障害、自閉症・情緒障害・特別支援学校：障害のある子どものみを対象とした学校。専門性の高い教員、理学療法士・言語聴覚士などの専門スタッフが揃い、少人数・個別支援を受けられる通級と特別支援学級の最大の違いは「在籍する学級」です。通級は通常学級に在籍したまま一部の時間だけ特別な指導を受ける仕組みであるのに対し、特別支援学級は少人数学級を基本に、子どもに合わせた学習・生活支援を受ける仕組みです。また通級指導教室では知的障害のある子どもは対象外とされている点も大きな違いです。参考：https://junior.litalico.jp/column/article/126/参考：https://h-navi.jp/column/article/35025660参考：https://www.yuineko.com/article/202607/shien-kyu-tsukyu-chigai/参考：https://specialeducationjourney.com/special-needs-school/特別支援学級を設置している学校の割合は、2015年時点で小学校の79.5％、中学校の75.5％にのぼり、多くの小中学校に設置されています。特別支援学級では、朝の会や体育・音楽・給食などの時間だけ通常学級に参加する「交流学級」「共同学習」を実施している学校もあります。参考：https://yotsuyagakuin-ryoiku.com/jiheisyou/tokubetsushien.htmlなお発達障害（学習障害・注意欠如多動症）については、主に通級指導教室や通常学級での配慮による対応が想定されていますが、自閉症・情緒障害などを合併する場合は特別支援学級での教育が行われることもあります。参考：https://life.litalico.jp/hattatsu/mailmag/093/■7章 特別支援学級・支援を「どう勧めるか」――保護者への伝え方保育園・幼稚園の先生や、就学時健診の心理士から「支援学級を検討してみては」と言われたとき、多くの保護者は大きな衝撃を受けると言われています。「うちの子がどうして」「他の子と何が違うの」「普通じゃないということ？」といった不安、焦り、怒り、悲しみが一度に押し寄せることも少なくありません。参考：https://specialeducationjourney.com/criteria-for-entering-support-classes/このため、支援を勧める側（教員・支援者）には、以下のような配慮が求められます。・一方的な「診断」や「決定事項」としてではなく、子どもの育ちを共に考える相談として伝える・子どもの「できないこと」だけでなく「得意なこと・伸びしろ」もセットで伝える・特別支援学級・学校の制度やその後の進路（交流学級、通常学級への転籍、卒業後の進路など）について具体的な情報を示し、不安を減らす・保護者の意見を最大限尊重し、本人・保護者・学校・専門家が合意形成を行うプロセスを大切にする・一度の面談で結論を急がず、時間をかけて保護者が状況を整理できるようにする実際、就学先の決定については、「就学基準に該当する障害のある子どもは特別支援学校に原則就学する」という従来の仕組みが見直され、現在は障害の状態・本人の教育的ニーズ・本人と保護者の意見・専門家の意見・学校や地域の状況などを踏まえた「総合的な観点」から決定する仕組みに変わっています。市町村教育委員会が保護者に十分な情報提供を行い、保護者の意見を最大限尊重しながら合意形成を図ることが原則とされています。参考：https://www.mext.go.jp/b_menu/shingi/chukyo/chukyo3/siryo/attach/1325886.htm学校・先生と家庭の連携については、「合理的配慮はずるいのでは」「特別支援教育は差別では」といった周囲からの声にどう向き合うか、保護者が障害を受容できていない場合にどう関わるかなど、現場で起こりやすい具体的な悩みを扱った書籍・実践知も蓄積されています。参考：https://www.meijitosho.co.jp/detail/4-18-176345-9■8章 就学相談・就学先決定の流れ就学相談は、多くの自治体で年長児（就学前年）の春〜秋ごろから始まります。一般的な流れは以下の通りです。1. 相談の申し込み（保育園・幼稚園経由、または教育委員会へ直接）2. 面談・行動観察（子どもの日常生活、社会性、コミュニケーションなどについての聞き取りと観察）3. 発達検査・知能検査の実施（田中ビネー式、WISCなど）4. 教育委員会の会議での総合的な検討（本人・保護者の意見、専門家の意見、学校や地域の状況等）5. 就学先（通常学級／通級／特別支援学級／特別支援学校）の提案・合意形成6. 保護者への通知（市町村教育委員会が1月31日までに通知するなど、法令で時期が定められている）就学時健康診断は学校保健安全法に基づき11月30日までに実施され、その後、視覚障害・聴覚障害・知的障害・肢体不自由・病弱（身体虚弱を含む）に該当する子どもについては、市町村教育委員会が12月31日までに都道府県教育委員会へ通知し、都道府県教育委員会が1月31日までに保護者へ入学期日と就学先を通知する、という手続きが学校教育法施行令で定められています。参考：https://www.mext.go.jp/a_menu/shotou/shugaku/detail/1422234.htm参考：https://www.mext.go.jp/a_menu/shotou/tokubetu/002.htm就学相談で使われる発達検査・行動観察では、「社会性・行動」「日常生活」「コミュニケーション」といった観点でのチェックが行われます。「社会生活への適応が困難」とは、他人と関わって遊ぶ、決まりを守って行動するなどが、その年齢段階に一般に求められる程度に至っていない状態を指すとされています。参考：https://life.litalico.jp/hattatsu/mailmag/104/文部科学省は平成25年に作成した「教育支援資料」を改訂し、「障害のある子供の教育支援の手引」として、就学に関わる一連のプロセスとその趣旨を、関係者全体が理解できるよう整理しています。参考：https://www.mext.go.jp/a_menu/shotou/tokubetu/main.htm特別支援学級への入学基準（学校教育法に基づく）は、たとえば知的障害の場合「知的発達の停滞があって意思疎通や日常生活に援助を必要とする状態、または社会生活への適応が著しく困難な状態」とされています。参考：https://comotto.docomo.ne.jp/column/00000031-2/■9章 個別の教育支援計画・個別の指導計画特別支援教育の対象となる子どもについては、次の2種類の計画が作成されます。【個別の教育支援計画】教育機関が中心となり、家庭・医療・福祉など関係機関と連携して作成する、乳幼児期から学校卒業後までを見通した長期的な支援計画です。本人・保護者の願い、障害による困難な状況、学校での支援・指導内容、合理的配慮の提供状況、生育歴、相談歴、福祉サービスの利用状況などが盛り込まれます。作成プロセスは自治体や学校によって異なりますが、一般的には「本人・保護者へのヒアリング→関係機関へのヒアリング（保護者の了承のうえ）→計画案の作成→共有・合意形成」という流れをたどります。参考：https://h-navi.jp/column/article/35028242参考：https://www.mext.go.jp/a_menu/shotou/tokubetu/material/1340250_00005.htm【個別の指導計画】個別の教育支援計画を踏まえ、教育課程における目標・指導内容・指導方法をより具体的にするために作成される計画です。単元や教科、学期ごとに作成し、定期的に指導の成果を評価しながら、その都度見直していきます。学習指導要領にも「障害のある児童などについては、学習活動を行う場合に生じる困難さに応じた指導内容や指導方法の工夫を計画的、組織的に行うこと」が明記されています。参考：https://www.pref.niigata.lg.jp/uploaded/attachment/212030.pdf参考：https://www.mext.go.jp/a_menu/shotou/tokubetu/material/1298214.htm■10章 合理的配慮の考え方と具体例2016年4月に施行された障害者差別解消法により、公立学校を含む行政機関には、障害のある子どもへの合理的配慮の提供が義務化されています（2024年からは事業者にも義務化）。合理的配慮とは、障害者権利条約の定義によれば「障害者が他の者との平等を基礎として人権及び基本的自由を享有・行使することを確保するための必要かつ適当な変更及び調整であって、均衡を失した、または過度の負担を課さないもの」とされています。参考：https://famicare.jp/2023/12/16/reasonable-accommodation/参考：https://www.kyoiku-press.com/post-228477/具体例としては、次のようなものが挙げられます。・読み書きに困難がある子には、拡大教科書やタブレット、音声読み上げソフトの利用を認める・刺激に敏感で集中しづらい子には、仕切りのある机や別室でのテスト受験を用意する・指示理解に困難がある子には、指示を一つずつ出す、予定をカードや表で視覚的に示す・肢体・視覚が不自由な子には、介助者や補助具の使用を認める参考：https://junior.litalico.jp/about/hattatsu/consideration/合理的配慮を提供するまでの流れは、おおむね次の通りです。1. 本人・保護者が家庭内で状況や希望を話し合う2. 特別支援教育コーディネーターや学級担任に「意思の表明」をする3. 学校が校内支援委員会で実態把握を行う4. 本人・保護者も参加する個別のケース会で内容を検討・調整する5. 内容を個別の教育支援計画に記載し、関係者で共有する6. 校内で共通理解を図り、環境整備を経て提供を開始する7. 提供後は定期的に見直しを行い、必要に応じて進路先へ引き継ぐ参考：https://www.mext.go.jp/content/20211011-mxt_tokubetu01-000018372_02.pdf千葉県教育委員会など、自治体単位で具体的な合理的配慮の事例集を公開しているところもあります。参考：https://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/shien/tokubetsushien/gouritekihairyojireishuu.html参考：https://www.pref.chiba.lg.jp/kyouiku/shien/tokubetsushien/gouritekihairyojireishuu-highsuchool.html■11章 早期療育・児童発達支援センターの活用就学前の段階から利用できる公的な支援の代表が「児童発達支援」です。児童発達支援には、地域の中核的な療育支援施設としての機能を持つ「児童発達支援センター」と、身近な療育の場である「児童発達支援事業」の2種類があります。センターは、通所利用の子どもとその家族への支援に加え、地域の障害児やその家族への相談、保育所など子どもを預かる施設への助言も行う、地域のハブ的な存在です。参考：https://visit.aiai-cc.co.jp/column/jido-hattatsu-shien-center-guide/参考：https://job-medley.com/tips/detail/12917/こども家庭庁がまとめた「児童発達支援ガイドライン」では、発達支援の入口として幅広い相談に対応し、必要に応じて適切な支援につなげる機能や、こどもが安心して過ごせる居場所を提供し、生涯にわたるウェルビーイングの基礎を培うことが目標として位置づけられています。乳幼児健診や親子教室など、他の施策・機関とも連携しながら、「発達に不安を感じ始めた段階」の家族にも丁寧に対応することが重視されています。参考：https://www.cfa.go.jp/assets/contents/node/basic_page/field_ref_resources/7692b729-5944-45ee-bbd8-f0283126b7db/863f5ecf/20241101_policies_shougaijishien_shisaku_guideline_tebiki_02.pdf児童発達支援センターは、保健所・病院、発達障害者支援センター、障害児相談支援事業所、保育所・幼稚園、小学校、特別支援学校などの関係機関と連携し、子どもと保護者が円滑に支援につながり、その後も保育所や学校へ適切に支援が引き継がれるようにする役割を担っています。参考：https://www.mhlw.go.jp/file/06-Seisakujouhou-12200000-Shakaiengokyokushougaihokenfukushibu/0000171670.pdf■12章 卒業後の進路・その後の支援制度特別支援学級・特別支援学校卒業後の進路は、子どもの状態や本人・家族の希望によって多岐にわたります。小学校の特別支援学級卒業後は、中学校の特別支援学級、通常学級、特別支援学校中学部などへの進学が主な選択肢です。参考：https://comotto.docomo.ne.jp/column/00000031-2/成人期に向けては、以下のような就労・生活支援の制度があります。・就労移行支援：一般企業への就職を目指し、訓練や職場探しの支援を受ける・就労継続支援（A型・B型）：すぐに一般就労が難しい場合に、支援を受けながら働く経験を積む・ハローワーク：地域の求人情報と、障害のある方向けの専門相談窓口・障害者就業・生活支援センター：就労と生活の両面を一体的に支援する機関（全国337か所、2023年8月時点）参考：https://www.ajscrum.co.jp/business/job-assistance/column/moderate-intellectual-disability-support/参考：https://www.welbe.co.jp/campus/list/厚生労働省の調査によると、知的障害のある人が最も多く従事している産業は製造業で、卸売業・小売業、医療・福祉、サービス業が続いています。参考：https://www.cocorport.co.jp/jobs/column/intellectual_disability_job/■13章 相談窓口一覧【発達障害者支援センター】各都道府県・政令指定都市に1か所以上設置されており、本人だけでなく家族や関係者のみでの相談も可能です。相談支援、発達支援、就労支援の3つの機能を持ちます。全国一覧は以下から確認できます。参考（内閣府まとめ）：https://www8.cao.go.jp/shougai/whitepaper/h29hakusho/zenbun/gaibu/www_rehab2.html参考（国立障害者リハビリテーションセンター 全国一覧）：https://www.rehab.go.jp/ddis/action/center/参考（日本自閉症協会）：https://www.autism.or.jp/consultation/【国立障害者リハビリテーションセンター「家族支援」ページ】ペアレント・プログラムやペアレント・トレーニングに関する資料（事業化マニュアル等）を公開しています。参考：https://www.rehab.go.jp/ddis/howto/parents/【障害者就業・生活支援センター】就労と生活の両面から支援を行う全国の窓口です。お住まいの地域のセンターへの問い合わせが基本になります。■14章
