items.body: ＜Review＞ 上岡敏之×大阪交響楽団 シューマン交響曲全曲演奏会［Vol.1］ 若々しい抒情、豊かな「歌」 text by 増田良介 photo ©︎樋川智昭 上岡敏之指揮 大阪交響楽団 シューマン交響曲全曲演奏会［Vol.1］ 2026年6月18日（木）19:00 大阪・箕面市立メイプルホール 大ホール シューマン：交響曲第1番《春》 シューマン：交響曲第4番 迷いながら、あたりを窺いつつ出てくる《春》 箕面はいい街だ。市街地のすぐ北に、有名な大滝のある箕面国定公園があり、北摂山地の山麓には閑静な高級住宅地が広がる。飲食店もいい店がたくさんあって街歩きも楽しい。さて、そんな箕面が、このところ音楽でも注目を集めている。遠くからでも聴きに行きたくなるような魅力的な演奏会がいろいろと企画されているのだ。 その中心的な会場が、1988年にできた箕面市立メイプルホールだ。阪急箕面駅から徒歩10分のところにある、いわゆる多目的ホールで、筆者も、桂米朝一門会などで何度か行ったことがあったが、オーケストラの演奏会は、最近になるまで聴いたことがなかった。 ところが近年のメイプルホールは違う。大きな話題となった、坂入健司郎指揮大阪交響楽団によるブラームス交響曲全曲演奏会（2022～2024年）あたりから、魅力的な演奏会の企画が立て続けに行なわれているのだ。2025年11月には大阪フィルが公演を行なったのだが、指揮は、なんと今をときめくカーチュン・ウォンだった。そして今年からは、上岡敏之が大阪交響楽団を指揮してシューマンの交響曲全曲演奏会をやる！ これは聴き逃せない。 ということで、6月18日（木）に行なわれた第1回の演奏会を聴いてきた。曲目はシューマンの交響曲第1番と第4番。番号は離れているが、実は1番目と2番目に書かれた交響曲だ。曲線の美しいホワイエを通り抜けてホールに入ると、あらためて舞台と客席の近さを感じる。それもそのはず、このホール、大ホールでも客席は501席しかないのだ。それに対して、舞台の間口（横幅）は初台の東京オペラシティ コンサートホールとほぼ同じ、奥行きは初台よりさらに長い、と、奥田佳道さんがプレトークで言っていた。そんなホールにオーケストラを呼ぶのは採算的には大変なのだろうが、聴く方にとってはぜいたくな体験だ。 肝心の演奏はどうだったか。わくわくしながら交響曲第1番《春》の最初の音を待つ。始まって驚いた。あのファンファーレが、勢いよく飛び出す感じではなく、柔らかく控えめ、あえて言えば弱々しいのだ。「ドイツは日本と違って、寒い冬からある日一気に春になる、この曲の冒頭はそれを表わしているのだろう……」というような説明をときどき見るが、ドイツに長く暮らす上岡の演奏は、まったく一気ではない。むしろ、迷いながら、あたりを窺いつつ出てくる。 この変ロ長調のファンファーレは、和声が付いてもう一度繰り返されるが、これも晴れきらない。だが、このファンファーレを受けるのが、ラーーソファーミーレーというニ短調のフレーズであることを思えば腑に落ちる。そもそも、この時点ではまだ、春は完全に目を覚まし切っていないのだ。なるほど、と思う。もうこれで完全に上岡マエストロの掌の上だ。 さて、序奏が終わってアレグロ・モルト・ヴィヴァーチェの主部に入る。ここはさすがに完全に明るく力強い春の音楽になっているのだが、聴き慣れた演奏とはどうも様子が違う。第1主題の最初の部分の音符には全部スタッカートが付いているのだが、上岡はこれらの音を短く切るのではなく、テヌート気味に個々の音をしっかり伸ばして弾かせる。スタッカートとテヌートの扱いは上岡がどの曲でもこだわっているポイントだが、個人的には、思いもよらなかったところから、豊かな「歌」が聴こえてきて、とても新鮮だった。 先入観にとらわれず、緻密に作り上げていく さて、後半は第4番だ。オーケストラの一体感や呼吸感は第1番よりもさらに強まっている。こちらもテヌートを利かせ、個々の音が後を引くような歌い方が耳に残るが、作品の性格の違いか、第1番のように耳慣れない感じではない。だが、ときどきテンポの扱いが独特で、特に、第3楽章のトリオ、第2楽章の主題が出てくるところで、かなり速めのテンポを取っていたのは印象的だった。ここは第2楽章に合わせてやや遅くする演奏もあるが、テンポの指示はないからスケルツォ主部のテンポでそのまま行くのが筋なわけだ。 個人的な趣味で細かい話ばかり書いてしまったが、そういうことを気にせずとも、両曲ともシューマンの魅力を存分に引き出した、若々しい抒情がたっぷり伝わってくるすばらしい演奏だったことは強調しておこう。きっとそれは、先入観にとらわれず、細部までていねいに楽譜を読み直し、緻密に演奏を作り上げていく上岡の姿勢が、熱い情感のこもった演奏を持ち味とする大阪交響楽団と呼応して実現したものだろう。演奏時間は短かったが、大満足でホールを後にした演奏会だった。 ところで最初に書いたように、箕面は山に近い自然豊かな街だ。もしかすると、土地勘のない人には、大阪の中心部からかなり遠い場所という印象を持たれるかもしれない。しかし実際には、箕面駅から大阪梅田駅まで、阪急で30分もかからない。便利な場所なのだが、これはつまり、関西の音楽文化の中心であるザ・シンフォニーホールやフェスティバルホールや兵庫県立芸術文化センターにも1時間以内で行けるということを意味する。クラシック音楽好きが多いと言われる箕面市だが、メイプルホールはこれらの一流ホールと競わなければならないわけだ。しかし6月18日の客席には、地元の人たちはもちろん、大阪市内のホールでよく見かけるコンサート・ゴーアーの人たち、さらには東京など遠くから来た人たちも見受けられた。新企画の第1回、まずは大成功だったと言ってよいだろう。 なお、このシリーズ、第2回は2027年6月にシューマンの第2番とメンデルスゾーンの《スコットランド》、最終回は同年12月にシューマンの《ライン》とマーラーの交響曲第10番～《アダージョ》（！）と、強力な二の矢、三の矢が控えている。メイプルホールの快進撃はまだまだ続きそうだ。 公演情報 《身近なホールのクラシック》 上岡敏之指揮 大阪交響楽団 シューマン交響曲全曲演奏会 ［Vol.2］ 2027年6月4日（金）19:00 箕面市立メイプルホール 大ホール メンデルスゾーン：交響曲第3番《スコットランド》 シューマン：交響曲第2番 ［Vol.3］ 2027年12月3日（金）19:00 箕面市立メイプルホール 大ホール マーラー：交響曲第10番〜《アダージョ》 シューマン：交響曲第3番《ライン》 主催：公益財団法人箕面市メイプル文化財団 後援：箕面市／箕面市教育委員会／タッキー８１６みのおエフエム 協賛：大和ハウス工業株式会社 助成：一般財団法人地域創造

items.body: 「しかくい『え』はきらいなんだもん」。休みの日、3歳の子どもを美術館に連れて行こうとすると、こう言われてしまった。自分の身体で感じたことを通して世界を知っていく子どもにとって、壁に掛かった四角い絵のなかでは、世界はすでに完結しているように見える。そこには、自分の身体を差し挟む余地がない。「なんかいいこと言うね」と、その言葉を心に留めておいた。 7月に訪れた「小林重予×田中千智展 焦がれる─白い国、南方の風」（アートスペース貘、6月29日〜7月12日）と牛島智子「タマノ井 Bear3 ト うちうし本」（福岡県立美術館 展示室4、6月30日〜7月5日）はいずれも福岡拠点の作家による展示だ。二つの展示はまったく異なる方法で、どちらも「しかくい『え』はきらい」という言葉に呼応するように感じられた。一方は完結した世界の中に生命を宿し、もう一方はフレームそのものを空間へほどいていた。   閉ざされた空間への誘い──「小林重予×田中千智展 焦がれる─白い国、南方の風」 「アートスペース貘（ばく）」は親不孝通りにある喫茶店「屋根裏貘」の一角を占める。1977年の開業以来、近隣の学生や表現者たちの通う憩いの場だ。私はいまだ喫茶スペースには少し気後れしてしまうが、左手奥のギャラリーには何度も足を運んでいる。入り口の看板にはマジックで展示タイトルが書かれている。階段を上って薄暗い店内に入る。街の喧騒から切り離された、閉じた雰囲気が、作品への没入を促す場所だ。 本展の作家である田中千智と2017年に亡くなった小林重予は、実際に対面したことはなかったようだが、今回の二人展では、壁に掛けられた作品同士が呼応し、お互いに境界を越えようとしているように感じた。 「小林重予×田中千智展 焦がれるー白い国、南方の風 」展示風景［筆者撮影］ 田中は、「日常の中で出会ったものや感じたこと」をもとに制作した水彩ドローイングや、風景や人物、植物をテーマに描いた油彩画を、新旧とり混ぜて展示していた。アクリル絵の具で黒を背景とした静かな心象風景とともに、小林の作品と呼応するような、種をモチーフにした作品もこの中には含まれていた。 なかでも、雪の降る林の中で人物が描かれている作品はさわやかだった。芽吹きを待つ植物のような形が、画面のあちこちに現われていた。雪解けとともに新しい命が顔を出す、その一瞬を見つめているようだった。小さな絵画が額縁に納められ、リズミカルに壁を彩る様子に、「しかくい『え』」発言を思い出した。フレームとはなんだろう。少なくとも、田中の作品にとってそれは窮屈なものには感じられない。さりげない情景がちりぢりになるのを留める役割を果たし、見る者を絵画の世界に誘うように見えた（田中作品に特徴的な色である黒も、その役割の一端を担っているかもしれない）。 「小林重予×田中千智展 焦がれるー白い国、南方の風 」展示風景［筆者撮影］ 対照的に、小林の作品には、額縁に収められていてもなお、画面の外へ伸びようとする生命力があった。2年間のインドネシア滞在でバリ絵画と木彫を学んだという彼女の作品を、筆者は福岡市美術館の所蔵品以外は知らずにいたが、初めて今回じっくりと鑑賞することができた。小林は、活動していた期間にさまざまな素材を組み合わせ、植物のような形を生み出した。光を受けてきらめく表面は、柔らかそうで、みずみずしい。しかし同時に、毒や棘を思わせる攻撃性も孕んでいる。植物のようでありながら、生き物の臓器にも見えるそれらは、画面の外へと這い出しこちらへ迫ってきそうな気配を漂わせる。額縁は、その生命力をかろうじて留め、作品としての均衡を保っていた。 「小林重予×田中千智展 焦がれるー白い国、南方の風 」展示風景［筆者撮影］   編集され続ける風景──「タマノ井 Bear3 ト うちうし本」 「タマノ井 Bear3 ト うちうし本」は、福岡県立美術館の展示室を借りて行なわれた牛島智子の自主企画だ。展示室には、いくつかの小さな絵画、祖父母の代から使われてきた布団や衣類などの古布をはぎ合わせたタペストリー（「幕絵」）、八女和紙・蒟蒻のりを使用したオブジェが点在していた。 牛島の展示には、いつも過去作と新作が混在している。今回も、2026年春に福岡県福津市の旧玉乃井旅館で開催された「拍する家」★1の作品群が、新作とともに再配置されていた。牛島は2011年以来、玉乃井で天井画を手がけるなど、作品発表を重ねてきた。帽子をかぶり、難しい顔で本を読む人物の像は、かつて玉乃井の館主であった安部文範（2022年没）と重なって見えた。 「タマノ井 Bear3 ト うちうし本」展示風景［筆者撮影］ 会場を進むなかで、いくつかハッとする要素があった。ひとつ目は、三角形・四角形・多角形を組み合わせた立体物だ。入り口のある「家」と「庭」のような形を成しており、「家」をテーマにしてきた牛島の真骨頂といえる造形である。しかし、その表面に印象的に用いられた赤・黒・白の3色は、鶴岡正男の《人間気化》（1953年、宮城県美術館蔵）を連想させた。どこか血飛沫のような重々しさを持つビジュアルだ。 「タマノ井 Bear3 ト うちうし本」展示風景［筆者撮影］ 《人間気化》は原爆投下によって人間の身体が蒸発する様子を描いた作品だが、牛島の展示にも戦争への言及があった。サイコロの形のオブジェには「NO WAR」「戦争反対」の文字が書かれている。牛島は以前から蒟蒻のりと八女の和紙を用いてオブジェを制作してきたが、これが戦時中に少女たちが制作に従事した兵器「風船爆弾」の材料であることを知り、以前から関心を抱いていたという。小規模ながらアメリカ本土で実際の被害を出したこの兵器は、北九州市の小倉陸軍造兵廠で製作されていた。牛島は小倉市の戦争資料館に通い、実際に和紙の構造物を空中に飛ばす実験まで行なったそうだ。だらんと垂れ下がった茶色い大きな袋状の物体は、一見すると大きな牛の胃袋のようにも見えたが、牛島なりに風船爆弾を表現し、今の時代に反戦の意志を示そうとした試みだった。 次に注目したいのが、タイトルにも掲げられている「うちうし本」だ。牛島は八女市の自宅を拠点に、随時、壁新聞や小規模な出版を重ねている。2025年からは、自身のドローイングのシリーズを製本した冊子を制作する活動をはじめ、今回、それらが一堂に会していた。紙の帯を潜らせた装丁など、私にとって初めて見る書籍の形態だった。会場では、過去に制作された冊子をさらに合本にし、「ほうき」「筆」「蝋燭」の3種類のいずれかのドローイングを表面に施した冊子を購入することもできる。牛島の制作補助を2024年から行ない、福岡市内にある製本工房「1F右」で製本を学ぶ内山けい子が担当したという。 「タマノ井 Bear3 ト うちうし本」展示風景［筆者撮影］ この展示を見ながら、ラジオ番組「OUR CULTURE, OUR VIEW」★2で耳にした対話を思い出した。「ページ」という形式には、領域を展開する力があるという話だ。本は綴じられているからこそ、読むたびに開かれ、新たなコミュニティを生み出す。その考え方は、展示を絶えず編集し続ける牛島の実践とも重なっている。 これらの作品は、壁だけに留まっていない。床へ直に置かれていたり、一部留められてだらんと垂れ下がったりしている。これらのいったモチーフは互いに呼応しながら、空間へと広がっていった。 総じて、この展示にはたびたび四角が現われるのだが、その輪郭は緩やかだ。額縁、ページ、立方体、家といったフレームは、何かを閉じ込めるためではなく、人や場所、記憶をつなぎ直すための形式として現われている。また床というフレームは通路ではなく、鑑賞者を作品の世界に取り込むための舞台になる。鑑賞者は自然と足元へ目を落とし、歩く速度を変え、作品の間を縫うように身体を動かす。そこではフレームは作品を閉じ込めるものではなく、その身体を展示へ迎え入れるための一つの節点となっていた。   子どもが「きらい」と言っていたのは、絵画ではなく自分の身体が入り込めない鑑賞の形式だった。 壁をどう使い、床をどう使い、境界をどのように立ち上げるのか。その選択によって、展示に身を置いた鑑賞者と作品との距離は変わる。四角いフレームは、作品を閉じ込めるためだけのものではない。その外側へ身体や想像力を送り出すための装置にもなりうる。 そう考えると、「しかくい『え』はきらい」というあの一言は、絵画への拒絶ではなく、美術を鑑賞する空間そのものへの、小さく鋭い批評だったのかもしれない。 ★1──「拍する家」、旧玉乃井旅館（福岡）、2026年4月29日〜5月24日。 ★2──福岡のラジオ局「LOVE FM」で放送されているラジオ番組。太宰府天満宮で開かれたアートブックフェア「Pages | Fukuoka Art Book Fair 2026」をめぐる特集で、福岡の出版社や書店主たちがローカルなパブリッシングについて語っていた回（2026年5月10日放送）での、尾中俊介（Calamari Inc.）の発言。 小林重予×田中千智展 焦がれる─白い国、南方の風 会期：2026年6月29日（月）〜7月12日（日） 会場：アートスペース貘（福岡県福岡市中央区天神3-4-14） タマノ井 Bear3 ト うちうし本 会期：2026年6月30日（火）〜7月5日（日） 会場：福岡県立美術館 展示室4（福岡県福岡市中央区天神5-2-1） 詳細URL：https://fukuoka-kenbi.jp/exhibition/2026/0305_18380/

items.excerpt: 会期：2026/05/15～05/24 会場：BONUS TRACK GALLERY 2［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://note.com/bonustrack_skz/n/neb95ed6a0dca （前編より） では作為性そのものを駆け引きの対象にするようなこの「組み木ペインティング」は、どのように作られているのだろうか。その鍵を解くのは「AI」である。小田島によると、これらのシリーズの制作手順は次の通りだ。まずデジタルでドローイングを行ない、それをAIに読み込ませる。次に自身の過去作を学習させ、プロンプトを指示する。そこで出来上がったイメージを線画に変換し、2016年の個展「アイロニカルな肯定、その愛。」（TETOKA）でも使われたレーザー加工機で支持体を分割する。それを組み木として再構成しながら、AIが出力したイメージを作者自身で再編集・再構成するようにして一群の作品は完成するという。 「HEAD LUX KISS」展示風景［写真：皆藤将（美学校）］ 細かな部分は小田島の判断も入っているとのことだが、このように「組み木ペインティング」はAIを制作過程に組み込むことによって
items.body: 会期：2026/05/15～05/24 会場：BONUS TRACK GALLERY 2［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://note.com/bonustrack_skz/n/neb95ed6a0dca （前編より） では作為性そのものを駆け引きの対象にするようなこの「組み木ペインティング」は、どのように作られているのだろうか。その鍵を解くのは「AI」である。小田島によると、これらのシリーズの制作手順は次の通りだ。まずデジタルでドローイングを行ない、それをAIに読み込ませる。次に自身の過去作を学習させ、プロンプトを指示する。そこで出来上がったイメージを線画に変換し、2016年の個展「アイロニカルな肯定、その愛。」（TETOKA）でも使われたレーザー加工機で支持体を分割する。それを組み木として再構成しながら、AIが出力したイメージを作者自身で再編集・再構成するようにして一群の作品は完成するという。 「HEAD LUX KISS」展示風景［写真：皆藤将（美学校）］ 細かな部分は小田島の判断も入っているとのことだが、このように「組み木ペインティング」はAIを制作過程に組み込むことによって出来上がっている。かつてマーシャル・マクルーハンは「私たちは道具を形づくり、その後、道具が私たちを形づくる★2」という言葉を残したとされるが、小田島ほど、この言葉の後半部分「道具が私たちを形づくる」というテーゼを体現しているクリエイターはいないだろう。彼はそのデザインワークにおいても、絵をコピー機にかけ、荒れた状態をあえて作り出すことで「機械の使い方のバグ的というか、隙間的なものを楽しんでるんです★3」と語っている。 しかもその「道具」が、どのような出自を持つものでも構わないという平等性も彼の特徴だ。小田島はくるりなどさまざまなミュージシャンの作品のデザインを手がけているが、ここで言及したいのは、サニーデイ・サービスのアルバム『東京』（1996）のジャケットデザインである。水辺に咲く満開の桜が大きくレイアウトされた同作であるが、実はこの図版はアルバム用に撮影されたものではなく、植物図鑑から取られたものである。小田島は図鑑の白い桜をカラーペンでピンクに塗って、ジャケットを完成させた。ここにおいて明らかになるのは、道具として何を選ぶかという「サンプリング」が、デザインにおける重要な要素となっていることである。 もちろん、こうした美意識は小田島が音楽、現代美術に薫陶を受けるなかで育まれたものであるが、日本のグラフィックデザインに話を限定すると、アートディレクターの信藤三雄の仕事とも共鳴するだろう。信藤は1990年代の渋谷系やJ-POPのミュージシャンのCDジャケットのデザインで知られている。彼は過去の音楽を引用、編集することに積極的だった渋谷系ミュージシャンに呼応するかのように、ピート・モンドリアンやファッション誌『VOGUE』の写真など、有名無名問わず、さまざまな過去の表象を用いてデザインを行なっていた。 このような意味で小田島は、信藤と同様90年代の音楽シーンにおいて時代を象徴するビジュアルイメージを作り出してきた存在だと言えるだろう★4。しかしそれ以上に、「組み木ペインティング」への分析を経て重視すべきなのは、そのキャッチーな仕事の基底にある「方法」へのこだわりこそが、彼のクリエイターとしての根本であるということである。LLMを通過した一回性の絵画は、ポップ・アートの重要な一要素でもあるコンセプチュアルな側面を顕在化させる。つまり小田島の取り組む「アノニマスポップ」とは、匿名性を起点としながらも、最終的にはそれぞれの仕事に固有の値を立ち上げるような営みだったのである。 ★2──徳井直生『創るためのAI 機械と創造性のはてしない物語』（ビーエヌエヌ新社、2021、67ページ） ★3──前掲「イラストレーター・デザイナー 小田島等」 ★4──また、イラストレーション史上に小田島を位置づけるならば、スージー甘金との関係が重要になるだろう。本稿執筆に際してのやりとりのなかで、小田島はスージーを「パロディ」を背景に持つ作家であると述べ、自身は「サンプリング」「シュミレーション」であると語ってくれた。 参考資料 ・小田島等『ANONYMOUS POP 小田島等作品集』（スペースシャワーネットワーク、2010） ・コンテムポラリー・プロダクション『シーティーピーピーのデザイン』（光琳社出版、1996） 鑑賞日：2026/05/18（月）

items.body: 会期：2026/06/18～2026/09/21 会場：東京都写真美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://topmuseum.jp/exhibition/5417/ 日本におけるビデオアートとフェミニズム・アートの先駆者である出光真子は、娘・妻・母という役割がいかに女性へ割り当てられ、家族やマスメディア、社会制度を通じて差別が内面化されていくかを映像によって解剖してきた作家である。家庭という私的空間に潜む歪みを捉え直し個人の身体や欲望を規定する権力を露出させる映像作品群。東京都写真美術館での大規模回顧展では、出光の映像作家としての活動の軌跡を辿ることができる。 会場風景［筆者撮影］ 出光の出発点は1960年代後半のアメリカ生活にある。ニューヨークへ留学し、抽象表現主義のサム・フランシスと結婚して二児の母となった出光は、言語の壁のなかで言葉に代わる自己表現として映像を手にする。UCLAのエクステンション講座で8ミリ映画を学び、同時期にアメリカでウーマン・リブに触れながら、1972年にはジュディ・シカゴやミリアム・シャピロらによるウーマンハウスを撮影している。家庭を創作と政治の双方が交差する場所と捉える視点は、女性を従属的な役割へ閉じ込める社会構造の批判としてその後の実践にも一貫して受け継がれている。 展示の冒頭を飾る《主婦の一日》（1977）は、出光を代表する入れ子状の映像構造が明確に表われた作品である。家事労働に追われる主婦を演じる出光を画面内に置かれたテレビモニターの眼が絶えず見つめる映像は、均質な家族像を流通させるマスメディアによるイメージと外部から女性に向けられてきた規範的な眼差しを物質的に表わし、妻や母としての役割を自身に内面化する、内なる構造的な目線を露呈する。出光興産の創業者一族という特権的かつ家父長制的な環境に生まれた出光にとって、家庭という主題は抽象的な社会問題ではなく、自身の内外を貫く現実そのものである。性別による役割分業が明確な家父長制的環境のなかで、ビデオという新しいメディアを手に取り、家庭を内側から解剖していく。夫から息子へと欲望の対象を移しながら、息子を私物化する母親を描いた《やすしの結婚》（1986）は、抑圧された女性が、自ら家父長制を内面化し、やがて構造を再生産する加害的な主体になり得るというパラドックスを示す。 さらに、長姉・出光孝子の半生を下敷きにした《清子の場合》（1989）や、家事と労働に追われ、自身の創作を男性の権威特権によって妨げられる女性芸術家の不遇を描いた《加恵、女の子でしょ！》（1996）は、ジェンダーによる役割分業が家庭内にとどまらず、芸術という制度の内部にも根を下ろしている事実を露呈している。そこからは著名画家との結婚を経てアーティストになった出光自身の切実な日々が透けて見える。また本作であえて流用されるメロドラマのような過剰な語法——大げなBGM、カットの切り替え、感情的な編集作法——は、マスメディアによって再生産され、均質的に描かれる女性の表象を、映像メディアを通して倒錯的に批判するものである。《アニムス パート 2》（1982）でも、ネオダダの岸本清子の身体的なパフォーマンスを通して、女性の内部に想定された男性的な存在が異質な像として不気味に立ち現われる。 女性差別を痛烈に批判する出光の作品群を辿ると、制度への批判と同じくらい、女性の身体を役割や属性へと還元する記号化に抗う、生々しい身体感覚に目が向けられる。《Baby Variation》（1974）や《Something Within Me》（1975）では、ポップアートのような色彩で着色された生肉や、蠢くカタツムリといった触覚的なイメージが連鎖し、記号化から逸脱しようとする生理感覚や身体が軽快に躍動する。出光にとって最初のビデオ作品となった《おんなのさくひん》（1973）で映される使用済みの生理用品もまた、隠蔽されてきた身体の痕跡を美的対象へと引き上げ、規範化されない視点を差し出すものである。 本展の副題に掲げられた「ある映像作家の自伝」とは、自身を形づくった家族、制度、そしてメディアの統治構造を解体し、そのなかに生きる身体経験を映像を通して編み直すことでもある。私的空間の内部にカメラを持ち込み、娘・妻・母という役割を生み出す視線や欲望を可視化することで、出光は個人的な身体経験を社会的な権力の問題へと開いていく。そうした構造批判を往還する映像のあり方に出光真子の作品がもつ唯一性がある。 会場風景［筆者撮影］ 鑑賞日：2026/07/04（土）

items.album: Simi Fyda ~ In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn
items.excerpt: Simi Fyda‘s In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn offers no gentle introduction. Compared to Yuri (2023), it works within a noticeably narrower palette. The bright contrasts of its predecessor have given way to a largely monochrome world, built from minute variations of timbre, pressure and pitch. items.body: Simi Fyda‘s In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn offers no gentle introduction. Compared to Yuri (2023), it works within a noticeably narrower palette. The bright contrasts of its predecessor have given way to a largely monochrome world, built from minute variations of timbre, pressure and pitch. Many of the preoccupations of Yuri remain, but they are pursued with greater concentration. The music repeatedly folds back on itself, testing how much tension can be extracted from the smallest amount of material. The opening track, “-may-care”, signals a state of abrasion, establishing an atmosphere of metallic coldness that hangs over the entire record. “maso chords” introduces a faint current of nostalgia, its harmonies carrying the suggestion of something remembered yet irretrievable. From there, the material grows steadily more compressed. “idle hands” simmers without release, while “hedo chords” circles obsessively around recurring intervals and frozen harmonic figures. By the time “mono chords” arrives, repetition itself has become the subject. Minute tonal inflections slowly reshape the surface until the music seems to trap itself inside its own logic, producing a sense of claustrophobia without ever resorting to excess. Originally conceived as an octophonic installation before being reimagined for stereo, the music acquires an unusually enclosed character. Sounds seem unable to disperse, and repeated gestures linger, each return carrying greater psychological weight. Even the faint vocal traces remain caught within the surrounding texture, surfacing only briefly before dissolving back into the dense harmonic field. The closing “take the hindmost” provides the only substantial shift in perspective. Layers of electronic residue and circuitry redirect attention towards texture itself, as if searching for a new vocabulary from within the material already at hand. Nothing resolves. Instead, the album erases its own traces, leaving behind only the memory of sounds unwilling to disappear. The allow us to delve deeper into her personal heaven, Simi Fyda has kindly agreed to answer four questions by email. The album emerged from what you describe as “a version that almost existed” — music composed during a period of isolation and then reshaped into its final form. Could you talk about what was lost, what was retained, and whether you think traces of that unrealised version still haunt the record we hear today? I started the octophonic pieces during a period where I genuinely couldn’t make anything. I had no access to whatever I normally rely on. So I thought okay, let’s see if I still can do this. It was less of a decision and more just something to do, or to maintain. When I came back to it I was still kinda fed up with the whole thing, which actually helped. I stopped being careful with it and a lot got cut. But the atmosphere stayed, which annoyed me at first because I half wanted a clean break from it. I think that the earlier version is still in there somewhere, not as a foundation, probably more like the thing the record keeps almost touching without quite getting there. You have said that composing this music felt like becoming a demon — specifically one of the figures your grandmother claimed to have encountered in the very space where the album was eventually completed. How did that family story enter the work, and what does the title In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn reveal about the relationship between ancestry, memory, and self-transformation in your practice? I moved back into my grandmother’s apartment last November for a couple months and basically just disappeared into it. I wasn’t planning to make a record about any of that. I thought I was making something from a place rather than about it. She had paranoid schizophrenia, periods of seeing figures, demons, specific presences in specific corners of that apartment. I grew up hearing all of it, kind of terrified and fascinated at the same time. I lived there alone as a teenager too. So by the time I came back last november, it was already carrying a lot, I just wasn’t thinking about it consciously. She died in March, right after the album was finished. The timing still felt… I don’t even have a word to use here to be honest. The album isn’t about her, at least that wasn’t the intention. But she’s in there. Much of the album feels remarkably restrained. Tracks seem to hover on the verge of unleashing a full sonic assault, yet repeatedly pull back into themselves. Even the buried vocal traces feel half-suppressed, as though emerging from behind a wall. Was this tension between eruption and containment a conscious compositional strategy, or did it arise naturally from the material? Mostly conscious. I over-anticipate everything. I’ll have already resolved something in my head before it’s even happened, which just kills it. So a lot of this was genuinely trying not to do that. Whenever something felt like it was building toward release I’d just hold it there a bit longer than felt comfortable. I kept reminding myself that circling around something can be enough, that I don’t always have to arrive, don’t have to control every outcome in the ways I’ve conditioned myself to. The record is built around recurrence rather than development, with sounds, intervals, pipe tones and microtonal clusters reappearing in altered forms throughout the album. Given your background in installation and spatial sound, how did the process of collapsing an octophonic work into stereo affect your thinking about repetition, space and listening? Did reducing the physical dimensions of the piece paradoxically make it feel more intimate, claustrophobic, or psychologically charged? The recurrence came from spending a long time with a very small pool of material. At some point development just stopped making sense as a framework. Returning somehow did. In the octophonic versions sound could leave, it had a room to dissolve into. In stereo it couldn’t, so everything that was previously escapable became structural. The noise, the density, all of it just stayed there and then I brought it all even closer and it changed what the material actually was. I think space didn’t disappear, it just stopped being outside the work.

items.excerpt: Since first joining the n5MD roster in 2013, Zaragoza has consistently expanded the artistic possibilities of the Ocoeur project. items.body: Since first joining the n5MD roster in 2013, Zaragoza has consistently expanded the artistic possibilities of the Ocoeur project. Greener Grass, Clearer Water represents another significant step forward, demonstrating an artist increasingly comfortable allowing restraint, patience, and subtlety to become primary compositional tools. One of Ocoeur’s most thoughtful and engaging works to date Greener Grass, Clearer Water by Ocoeur   Ocoeur has steadily refined a distinct artistic voice over more than a decade of releases on the n5MD label, but Greener Grass, Clearer Water feels like a particularly meaningful milestone. Franck Zaragoza has long demonstrated an exceptional sensitivity to texture, atmosphere, and emotional pacing, yet his eleventh full-length reaches an impressive level of restraint that proves deeply rewarding. Zaragoza embraces spaciousness and patience, allowing every sustained tone and subtle harmonic shift to carry remarkable emotional weight. The result is one of his most thoughtful and engaging works to date. Following the ecological themes introduced on Breath, Greener Grass, Clearer Water expands that vision into a fully beatless landscape where every composition unfolds with quiet confidence. There is an understated elegance throughout the record that never feels static. Instead, Zaragoza continually reshapes the listening experience through carefully layered drones, delicate piano figures, luminous synthesizer washes, and nearly imperceptible changes in density. His background in both classical composition and cinematic scoring becomes immediately apparent, not through grand gestures but through his remarkable command of pacing and emotional nuance. The opening sequence establishes the album’s character beautifully. “Clouds Never Die” introduces a serene sonic environment built from slowly unfolding harmonic movement and restrained orchestral textures. Zaragoza allows themes to emerge naturally from the interaction between sustained tones and gentle timbral variations. “Tomorrow, The Birds Will Sing” continues this approach with remarkable poise, offering subtle shifts in color that evoke openness and possibility without becoming sentimental. What makes Greener Grass, Clearer Water so compelling is its confidence in simplicity. Zaragoza understands that meaningful expression often comes through what is omitted rather than what is added. Each composition feels carefully considered, with no unnecessary embellishment competing for attention. Silence becomes an active compositional element, giving individual sounds room to resonate fully before yielding to the next carefully placed gesture. Every composition unfolds with quiet confidence :: Tracks such as “Lumières” and “Le chemin du retour” highlight Zaragoza’s remarkable ability to balance warmth with restraint. Rich harmonic layers bloom gradually before dissolving into softer passages that maintain an almost tangible sense of openness. The production is immaculate throughout, revealing countless subtle details during repeated listens. Gentle reverberation, carefully sculpted frequencies, and seamless transitions create an immersive environment that rewards attentive listening without ever demanding it. The album’s environmental perspective is equally successful because it avoids overt statements. Rather than illustrating ecological concerns through dramatic contrasts or heavy-handed symbolism, Zaragoza communicates through atmosphere alone. These compositions present imagined spaces where natural processes unfold with quiet dignity, encouraging reflection without prescribing conclusions. The emotional impact emerges organically through the music itself, allowing listeners to engage with the underlying themes on their own terms. The centerpiece, “Remember the Sea,” beautifully demonstrates Zaragoza‘s mature compositional voice. Broad harmonic movements rise and recede like slow tides, while distant textural elements provide an ever-changing backdrop that remains understated throughout. The piece captures a remarkable sense of scale while maintaining intimacy, a balance that few artists working within contemporary ambient music consistently achieve. The second half continues to deepen the album’s emotional resonance. “What Are You Running After?” introduces subtle harmonic tension before resolving into passages of remarkable clarity, while “Silences” explores the expressive potential of negative space with extraordinary precision. Even during its quietest moments, the album remains fully engaging because Zaragoza continuously shapes the listener’s attention through microscopic adjustments in texture and dynamics. Silence becomes an active compositional element :: “Blue Sky and Golden Leaves,” “Let Go,” and the closing “Your Smile” complete the journey with remarkable grace. Rather than building toward a dramatic conclusion, Zaragoza allows the album to settle naturally into a state of quiet equilibrium. It feels entirely appropriate that the final moments arrive without spectacle, leaving behind an enduring sense of balance instead of resolution. Since first joining the n5MD roster in 2013, Zaragoza has consistently expanded the artistic possibilities of the Ocoeur project. Greener Grass, Clearer Water represents another significant step forward, demonstrating an artist increasingly comfortable allowing restraint, patience, and subtlety to become primary compositional tools. It also continues n5MD‘s long tradition of championing artists who explore the intersection of electronic composition, modern classical sensibilities, and immersive sound with exceptional care and craftsmanship. Repeated listens reveal new relationships between harmonies, textures, and spatial details that are easy to overlook initially. That lasting depth ultimately becomes the album’s greatest strength. Greener Grass, Clearer Water is not interested in immediate impact or dramatic statements. Instead, it invites careful attention, rewarding listeners with a richly detailed and emotionally resonant experience that continues to unfold long after the final notes disappear. It stands among Ocoeur‘s finest achievements and serves as another outstanding addition to n5MD‘s consistently exceptional catalog. Greener Grass, Clearer Water is available on n5MD. items.body: Cosmos in Collision‘s Unwound arrives two years after The Passage of Time and confirms the direction of an ever-evolving project, capable of building dense and cinematic atmospheres. The cover artwork is an original watercolor by Cosmos in Collision, visually translating the narrative arc of the record: three chromatic fields blending from indigo to black, crossed by a white thread that slowly thins until it disappears. A conceptual work deeply rooted in both the real and supernatural worlds Electronic instrumental sounds exploring the lines between sci-fi, ambient, electronica, post-rock and shoegaze, featuring layers of ethereal guitars, cinematic atmospheres, shimmering soundscapes and intricate rhythmic textures that are combined to create an evocative dreamlike flow of unnatural and entirely enchanting sound. Unwound is a conceptual work deeply rooted in both the real and supernatural worlds inspired by the myth of the Three Fates. Each has a different role in weaving the destiny of the collective constant listeners. They are shapeshifters and guardians of the pathways into the earth and of the “limit” frontiers where it is believed that the supernatural most freely manifests itself. The trio are generally conceived of as sisters and are often given the names Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, which are the names of the Moirai, the version of the Fates who appear in Greek mythology. This trio is also found in Vedic Ṛta, the Avestan Asha (Arta), and the Egyptian Maat, as well as throughout some of ancient Northern Europe. These divine figures are often artistically depicted as beautiful maidens with consideration to their serious responsibility, which is specifically the life of each mortal. The traditional role of the Three Fates is to ensure that every being, mortal and divine, lives out their destiny as it was assigned to them by the laws of the universe. Some would say that Lachesis sings of the things that were, Clotho the things that are, and Atropos the things that are to be. Clotho with thread, Lachesis with an eye glass, and Atropos with scissors. Throughout history, Time has been an important subject of study in religion, philosophy, and science, and perhaps most of all in Music. The universe is infinite, which is distinctly an obsession (and perhaps an exclusive illusion) of humans. Multiple notions exist, and defining time in a manner applicable to all fields without circularity has consistently eluded much of the traditional scholarship. Here, on the extended player Unwound, the Fates shape the temporal sonic destiny of each human, expressed in textile metaphors, hence spinning fibers into yarn, or weaving threads on a loom. Time (again) is a fundamental part of this musical universe, perceived by events happening in a sequence, in a dimension, the moment the thread starts to wind into a form for the warp and woof of existence. The first track, “Breath (Clotho)” (5:30) opens like a sunrise, with a melodic and ethereal theme, evoking the first breath, easing in as a melody starts, forming a circular repeating, and richer fuller thicker experience as we go deeper into outer space, wary of shadowy, background figures who only really ever reveal their fateful secrets to people at the moment that their fates actually come to pass. Clotho is often depicted as a younger woman because of her relationship with the birth of humans. Three chromatic fields :: Track 2, “Unwound (Lachesis)” (7:33), is the measured beating heart of the EP, a long journey through the highs and lows of existence, carried by rhythmic textures and ever-shifting soundscapes. For mortals, this destiny has spanned their entire lives and is represented as that thread spun from a spindle. Once the circles start spinning, slowly at first, we are in touch with deep space and though there is no dominating beat, there is a tempo in the cycles here. These are each different dancing snowflakes, which are so soon melted into the aggregate exquisite liquid details. These overlapping elements combine and conflict in different ways. Lachesis (the allotter) calibrates the life under judgement, measuring out and determining the length of human life as if it were a thread, in the natural order which regulates and coordinates the operation of the universe. The combined measurements mark a specific moment in time from a reference point, or epoch. Perhaps the only important parts of the natural order are birth and death, remembering that time is neither an event nor a thing, and thus is not itself measurable nor can it be travelled, except, of course, on occasion in dreams. Atropos is traditionally pictured as an old woman because of her hand in the death of mortals. “Severance (Atropos)” (4:19) closes the release with a painful crescendo culminating in the final cut, inevitable and silencing. Atropos chooses the manner of each person’s death, and when their time has come, she cuts their life-thread with her famously abhorred shears. The rotating and revolving melodic weave suggests pondering fatalism, or the subjugation of all events or actions to a universal destiny, and the acceptance of the inevitability of the natural order of things. As the universe expands, some humans say that it pulls time with it because space and time are somehow linked as one. Cosmos in Collision‘s Unwound arrives two years after The Passage of Time and confirms the direction of an ever-evolving project, capable of building dense and cinematic atmospheres. The cover artwork is an original watercolor by Cosmos in Collision, visually translating the narrative arc of the record: three chromatic fields blending from indigo to black, crossed by a white thread that slowly thins until it disappears. Cosmos in Collision is a musical journey of Riccardo Spaggiari, who is based in Italy. Unwound is available on Sun Sea Sky. items.body: Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Force and sweetness intertwined Operational Ambivalence by Somatic Responses   Brothers John and Paul Healy have been operating as Somatic Responses out of Ammanford, a small industrial mining community in southwest Wales, since 1994. They formed in the hardcore acid techno scene, releasing their first material in 1995 before gradually expanding into industrial, drum and bass, noise, ambient, and breakcore territory. Their 1999 debut Circumflex on Hymen Records was a pivotal moment—taking their sound into new levels of complexity and intensity, and subsequent releases on Ad Noiseam, Sublight, Component, and their own Photon Emissions label built one of the most expansive and underappreciated catalogs in hard-edged electronic music. Key influence on rhythmic noise, breakcore, and IDM, yet somehow always operating just below the mainstream radar. The duo describe their work as “complex dislocated and broken beats, distorted intelligent constructions, fascinating sonic structures, force and sweetness intertwined.” Operational Ambivalence, it’s worth noting, credits “Everything by J.S.Healy“—making this a solo John Healy production, recorded in the Macro Chamber in Ammanford, rather than a full duo effort. The distinction is subtle but real. What you get with Operational Ambivalence is largely what you’d expect from the Somatic Responses catalog: distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout. It’s a 14-track self-released collection that feels like a gathering of material that belongs together rather than a concept album with a rigid arc. Tracks 8, 9, and 14 are the more ambient pieces of the release and still create beautiful visual imagery through technique. Out of that ambient batch, “H doesn’t fall down the stairs…” is the most interesting—not strictly ambient like the other two, but considerably softer in production than everything surrounding it. The lightness and strange composition here is compelling in its subtlety, drum rhythm play with light percussion and glitched patterns that sit between experimental and delicate. Distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout :: “New Shift” is another standout, with its intro of rolling clicks and sounds moving left to right across the stereo field, slowly manipulated kick drums coming in gradually as the track builds rhythm. What you thought was a softer track reveals itself as something larger entirely. The technique of building anticipation through percussion here is notable, it recalls the way Lexaunculpt constructed his pattern builds of glitches and various percussions on The Blurring of Trees (Planet Mu, 2003), that same slow accumulation of rhythmic detail until the structure reveals itself. The patterns here are interesting and the execution is patient. “Gatch” is another standout in all of its distortion and drumming. What makes it work compositionally is how it messes with pattern recognition, introducing drum patterns that redirect where you expect the track to go. The distortion is toned down carefully, which is harder than it sounds. Somatic Responses have always been comfortable in distortion’s territory, and John Healy demonstrates that comfort here, using strong distortion without making ears bleed, keeping it controlled enough that it serves the composition rather than overwhelming it. Using strong distortion without making ears bleed :: “Vital Ex Parts 1 and 2” earns its nine-minute runtime—two parts that feel like one extended piece assembled well. The drums in the introduction are playful before they introduce harsher builds, eventually transforming into something darker with ambient surroundings closing in. And “Residual Behaviour” is the track that’s hardest not to stop at simply because of how oddly it stands out in the context of everything else. Real drum samples playing in broken patterns with chords filling in the background—it sounds off, but there’s a strange beauty to it. The double hits, the stutters, the subtle chords and notes behind the rhythm, there’s no steady pulse here, just experimentation. When a rhythm starts forming it plays briefly before switching again, until the track ends on skips and rolls and hi-hats leading the outro with swishy drums. It sounds like it was a genuinely fun track to make, and that energy comes through in the listening. Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Artwork once again by Mattia Travaglini, whose visual language has become as much a part of the Somatic Responses aesthetic as the music itself. Operational Ambivalence is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. A producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next Kine 3 by Roel Funcken   The golden era of IDM left behind a particular kind of silence, not the absence of music, but the absence of the restless, process-driven curiosity that made that era feel alive. What’s left of it now echoes through the electronic music landscape in small signals, from old and new artists working in the margins. Roel Funcken has been one of those signals for over two decades, and Kine 3 is his loudest transmission yet—a massive tracklist, a substantial runtime, and the third installment of an ongoing series that began as a way of making sense of a large body of work. The Kine series, released through EC Underground—the South Florida-based multidisciplinary collective and label that has been bridging European and UK electronic music to US audiences since 2018, operates on a process-first logic: raw, modular, driven by hardware and intention rather than polish and structure. My first encounter with Roel‘s work came through a college radio station playing Funckarma‘s Part 3 EP on Djak-Up-Bitch, the Rotterdam-based Dutch label specializing in modern electronica and IDM distributed through Clone. That particular series was something, the melodic play and drum work had a freshness that aged remarkably well, still sounds lovely today. Fast forward years later and here we land with Kine 3. This album shows the maturity of Roel as a solo artist, distinct from the Funckarma project that first put him on the map alongside his brother Don. His productions here aren’t built around melodic composition in the conventional IDM sense, they’re explorative and experimental, each track following a particular pattern of letting effects and drums do the talking while atmospheric or melodic backgrounds grind immersively in the background. The loop continues :: With a tracklist this expansive, the best approach is to section it. Tracks 1 through 8 share similarities in style and composition — drums and effects leading, melodies surfacing immersively rather than announcing themselves. What Funcken does here shouldn’t be misread as pure improvisation. It’s closer to freeplay with intention, a distinction that matters. Modular synthesis and process-driven production naturally produce moments that feel unplanned, but behind every patch decision is a set of deliberate choices: which modules are connected, what triggers what, where the randomness is allowed and where it’s controlled. Funcken‘s approach on Kine 3 sits in that exact space—the results sound alive and unpredictable but the architecture holding them together is clearly considered. Track 9, “4ehmth,” functions as a divider. It’s the only track of the bunch that’s almost entirely drum play, and whether intentional or not, it creates a natural break between the first and second halves of the album. “Bydow 32” carries a distinct Funckarma feeling—a reminiscence of “Atomic” or “Finsbury Park” from Part 3, those same loose, melodic textures surfacing again through a different production context. “Dorphins” is another standout. Its melodic structure separates itself from the rest of the batch because the tweaking of the melody is being granularized at fast speeds, bouncing on a single note with harsh portamento bend stabs cutting through. Portamento—the gliding between pitches rather than jumping discretely, becomes a compositional tool here rather than just an effect. When applied fast and aggressively, it creates a pitch tension that sits between melody and noise, which is exactly what Funcken is exploiting. The drum structure across all these tracks is consistently loose and abrasive, not a loop so much as one long continuous rhythm that plays through rather than repeating. The two bonus digital tracks round things out distinctly. “Koidz” is heavier—distorted drums, more rhythmically aggressive than the core album, with a crunchy acid bass and what sounds like significant knob movement throughout. The emotional pads that come in give it a melodic tone that sticks to the structure as it plays, a ringing atmospheric pad leading the melody in a way the main album rarely does. “Kido” takes the same sound palette and reconfigures it—a different melodic composition built from similar material but toned differently, another take on the same logic but with its own feel of rhythm and structure. Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. He noted that sitting back and listening to Kine 1 with an audience changed something: the distance it created meant he was actually listening rather than judging. The support those releases received went straight back into the system—new Eurorack modules, extending the loop. Kine 3 is what that loop sounds like three iterations in, and it sounds exactly like what it is: a producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next, documenting the results with the confidence of someone who’s been doing this long enough to know when to get out of the way and let the process speak. EC Underground found the right home for it. The loop continues. Kine 3 is available on EC Underground. items.body: Birmingham MC Admiral Jerry, born Jerry Butler, cut “Up and Coming MC” and “Demonstrate” with UB40 in 1985. He is back with “Chant Down Babylon”, out on Windrush Day, 22 June, the date the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury in 1948. Butler grew up in Handsworth, a first-generation Black Briton of Jamaican heritage. Grammar school and a private education came next. The racism did not. “Growing up in Handsworth as a first-generation Black Briton, I experienced plenty of racist attitudes at grammar school and throughout my education,” he says. “This song is for oppressed people everywhere who are hoping and striving for a better tomorrow.“ The lyrics name Kunta Kinte, George Floyd and the Windrush Generation. Jerry works the riddim as a toaster, chatting across a roots reggae backing in the old sound system manner. Aldo Dice produced the track at his Farda Dice Studios in Birmingham for The Empire Windrush EP, with Sovereign Tugz and See No Equal on the mix and master. Jah Mission, the Amsterdam production house, shot the video across Birmingham and London. It settles on the Benjamin Zephaniah mural in Handsworth Park, unveiled in honour of the poet and activist on Windrush Day in 2024, the year after his death. More music from Jerry arrives in early 2027. Stream “Chant Down Babylon” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Admiral Jerry – Chant Down Babylon appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — David has moved from Biblical themes (Earth Rot and his interpretation of Handel's Messiah) to a forceful Broadway-like production about the plight of the African-American slave. David has also moved from Capitol Records to MCA.1. "Oh! Freedom" (1:20) David's personal rendering (with the help of Billie Barnum's chorus) of a traditional Black spiritual of the most powerful kind. The arrangement is totally a cappella with feeling as much of being outdoors (like an in-the-fields spiritual) as it is that of a church performance by a Baptist Gospel choir. Wow! (Apparently this version of the song was the one used in the soundtrack of the television mini-series of Arthur Haley's Roots.) (4.75/5)2. "The Auction" (6:43) after opening with a bluesy BB King-like guitar intro, the band enters and settles into a very funky motif over which the guitarist continues for a bit before the voice of Fleming Smith enters with the support of "ah-oo" vocals from a full choir in his background, Fleming narrating the somber and horrific event of a slave auction. The guitars, bass, horn section, and lead saxophone continue on high funk trajectory as a singular female singer and full choir present lines about the scene between Fleming's narrative sections. The lead sax, lead guitar, and wah-wah and rhythm guitars are awesome in here as James Hughart's bass just slays it throughout. My only complaint would be not being able to always clearly distinguish the words being sung by the choir. (9.5/10)3. "Sympathy" (5:43) vocal soloist Jessica Smith (The Ikettes, The Mirettes) sings an emotionally-powerful plaintive vocal over some beautiful ballad-like supporting smooth jazz. These are great blues performances with a lovely capture of the feel (and acoustics) of a back-woods shack in the swampy South. Great support from the band and orchestra--especially from James Hughart's double bass, Ernie Watts' flute, and Joe Sample's electric piano. I love the use of Maya Angelou's "I know why the caged bird sings" reference in the lyrics. With a performance like this it is surprising to me that the world has not really ever heard of Ms. Jessica Smith. (9.25/10)4. "Freedom" (4:29) a female choir dirges over funky-bluesy electric piano-led music. The guitar solo in the second and third minutes is jazz-bluesy in a kind of BB King way. A male choir enters in the third minute to put in their two cents worth before a saxophone solo takes over (Ernie Watts?). Joe Sample is quite active and good throughout this though mostly beneath the action on top. A turn-taking male-female, solo and choir conversational "dialogue" supercedes the music in the final minute. A song that oozes passion and suffering. (9.25/10)5. "The Leading Citizen" (5:08) a very funky mostly-instrumental jam which is peppered with choral discourse (between the male and female choirs) before coming into instrumental sections presenting guitar and sax solos over the constant, insistent, hard-driving music. Though an excellent funk groove with great musicianship and pace, there is something lacking in the variety/variation department and melody. (Perhaps it has to do with the monotony of the hard-driving music and male-only choir singing about the white master.) Some amazing bass, drums, percussion, and wah-wah electric guitar (probably by Motown god, David T. Walker). (9/10)6. "The Debt" (4:19) a piano jazz combo sounds like it's playing inside an old Southern back-woods juke joint as a Alexander St. Charles (pseudonym for Benard Ighner) sings in a Joe Williams-like baritone. What a cool, time-capturing performance and piece! (9/10)7. "Be Proud-My Race" (4:43) this piano and horns-dominated jazz-funk piece sounds more like an Off-Broadway moral-religious piece (like Godspell or Jesus Christ Superstar) as the full choir (and I mean full) belts out the full and constant lyrics--which are, apparently, a full-text rendering of the lyrics as adapted from Paul Laurence Dunbar's poem "Ode to Ethiopia," which were first published in 1905. Every time I've listened to this I find myself weeping uncontrollably by the second verse. The one personal criticism/adaptation that I make are with regards to the electric guitar and sax flourishes made between verses: they feel totally superfluous and unnecessary, even discourteous, and 2) the fact that the song only covers the first five of the poem's ten verses."Ode to Ethiopia / Compensation"O Mother Race! to thee I bring This pledge of faith unwavering, This tribute to thy glory. I know the pangs which thou didst feel, When Slavery crushed thee with its heel, With thy dear blood all gory. Sad days were those ? ah, sad indeed! But through the land the fruitful seed of better times was growing. The plant of freedom upward sprung, And spred its leaves so fresh and young? Its blossoms now are blowing. On every hand in this fair land, Proud Ethiope's swarthy children stand Beside their fairer neighbour; The forests flee before their stroke, Their hammers ring their forges smoke, They sit in honest labour. They tread the fields where honour calls; Their voices sound through senate halls In majesty and power. To right they cling; the hymns they sing Up to the skies in beauty ring, And bolder grow each hour. Be proud, my race, in mind and soul; Thy name is writ on Glory's scroll In characters of fire. High 'mid the clouds of Fame's bright sky Thy banner's blazoned folds now fly, And truth shall lift them higher. Thou hast the right to noble pride, Whose spotless robes were purified By blood's severe baptism. Upon thy brow the cross was laid, And labour's painful sweat-beads made A consecrating chrism. No other race, or white or black, When bound as thou wert, to the rack, So seldom stooped to grieving; No other race, when free again, Forgot the past and proved them men So noble in forgiving. Go on and up! Our souls and eyes Shall follow thy continuous rise; Our ears shall list thy story From bards who from thy root shall spring, and proudly tune their lyres to sing Of Ethiopia's glory.Because I had loved so deeply, Because I had loved so long, God in His great compassion Gave me the gift of song. Because I have loved so vainly, And sung with such faltering [breath],The Master in infinite mercyOffers the boon of Death.Text Authorship: by Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872 - 1906), "Ode to Ethiopia"I do not know why David Axelrod always bulldozed his way into public controversy (the death of his mother at age eight, the many traumatic events he encountered on the streets of lower-class Los Angeles, his youthful career as a successful boxer, his own struggles with addiction) but I so admire his fearless willful expression of empathy and public attention for the causes of the disenfranchised, downtrodden, and marginalized. (9.5/10) 8. "Oh! Freedom" (0:34)Total time: 32:59A-/five stars; marked down for brevity this is still a very powerful piece of music--one that begs for recognition for its historical significance as well as for its fine composition, rendering, and performances.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — STATICA by Avenged Sevenfold is an interesting experiment that possibly may be a teaser for a new album or some sort of overall conceptual piece. Having dealt with scientific and philosophical themes on their last 2 albums, this seems to be a critique on AI music, especially with the overall presentation of the lyrics. While musically this is very different from what they normally present, there is some nice guitar playing. The autotune is annoying, but it is overall part of the supposed concept. But this isn't what I look for in this band, but I guess I commend their daring and enthusiasm. I'd give this a low to mid 6 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is ASHES.

items.body: Review by Matti — - The First Review -Following Memoria that was released in early 2026, this fourth album of the Finnish Psych/Space Rock group HADAL SHERPA is the second posthumous work, ie. recorded between 2021-2025 under the leadership of multi-instrumentalist and composer Vesa Pasanen (1982 - July 2025). In my review for Memoria I said it to be their best album, but this time around I cannot feel equally positive. Except for Vesa's cover art which is much better than on the two preceding albums. Musically, however, the band doesn't much show progress or fresh ideas. They firmly operate within the familiar formula of riff-based instrumental space rock with some Eastern nuances, thus falling into the subgenre's major trap of sounding the same as before.The 38-minute album has seven tracks. 'Camel on Moon' (no use exoecting allusions to the certain British prog classic) has a rich soundscape even if the composition is pretty predictable. Indeed Hadal Sherpa's strength definitely isn't versatility in song structures but in the fine details of arrangements, but that justifies things only to a certain degree, and the band doesn't bring anything new to the table in that sense either. The next three rather fast pieces feel all the same as they are built on powerful riffs and do not contain notable variety in the tempo.Within the very first slow seconds of 'Return to Farum Azul' I felt happily relieved: finally a track completely different from the others! This dreamy, atmosperic piece may not be progressive enough to be the finest compositions in the band's catalogue, but it easily is the highlight of this album. Pi Viana's wordless chant is a nice addition. 'Mountains' has some beautiful flute from Pi, and there's something charming in its relatively laid-back atmosphere. I came to think of spaghetti westerns even if the music doesn't resemble Morricone's.The seventh track 'Gurbet' is composed by �zdemir Erdogan of whom I know nothing. Hadal Sherpa has done good work covering this undoubtedly Turkish tune. Piirpauke comes to my mind for the groovy spirit. All in all the happy surprise are quite scarce on this album. Perhaps it had already come to the point of scraping the bottom of the barrel, to construct another full album from the posthumous recordings? In any case, this release was (at least for me) totally unexpected. The band has said they won't be making new music without their deceased primus motor. For fans and friends, naturally it was a happy surprise nevertheless.

items.body: Review by blessed_of — Compassionizer tribute to Depeche Mode is a sincere and beautifully crafted homage that captures the emotional depth and melodic power of the original songs, while reimagining them through the band's unique avant-prog and ambient sensibility. Instead of simply reproducing familiar material, Compassionizer opens new dimensions?experimenting with texture, rhythm, and atmosphere to make each piece feel newly discovered. "But Not Tonight" opens the album with a warm, dreamy atmosphere. Where Depeche Mode's version glows with youthful melancholy, Compassionizer transforms it into a reflective meditation. "World Full of Nothing" and "The Things You Said" follow with chamber-like arrangements and subtle electronics, preserving the emotional fragility of the originals while reframing them through the band's layered and expressive sound. "Blue Dress" maintains the sensual minimalism of Depeche Mode but becomes more introspective and ethereal, while "Sibeling" expands into a sweeping ambient dialogue between piano, clarinet, and electronic textures. The closing "Enjoy the Silence" stands not as a cover but as a reimagining?slower, sacred, and contemplative. Where Depeche Mode's originals thrive on sleek synth- pop precision, Compassionizer adds warmth, introspection, and organic depth, creating not imitation but an honest conversation across time and genres. A beautiful, thoughtful, and deeply moving album.

items.body: Review by blessed_of — This seven-track masterpiece has become a personal favorite, with its rich musical depth and immersive atmosphere. Two tracks, in particular, have made a lasting impression: "I Feel Shine of the Day" and "For the Invisible Things." These compositions stand out not only for their intricate arrangements but also for their ability to evoke powerful emotions and introspective moments. The album, as a whole, feels like an intricate journey, crafted with immense care and dedication. It's clear that Compassionizer has invested a great deal of effort, resources, and time into creating this project. From the very first note to the final soundscape, you can sense the precision and intentionality behind each element. The group's ability to weave together diverse sounds and moods is truly remarkable, giving each track its own unique character while maintaining a cohesive narrative throughout. One of the most striking aspects of "The Fellowship of the Mystery" is the band's ongoing evolution. With every album, Compassionizer continues to refine and expand their sound, pushing boundaries and experimenting with new ideas. Their growth as artists is evident in this latest release, which feels like a natural progression from their previous work while also introducing fresh and innovative elements. The compositions are more layered, the instrumentation more dynamic, and the emotional resonance even deeper than before. What I particularly love about this album is its ability to transport the listener into different emotional states. "I Feel Shine of the Day" is a radiant, uplifting track that seems to encapsulate the essence of hope and light, while "For the Invisible Things" taps into more subtle, introspective emotions. The contrast between these two pieces, and the way the album shifts between moods, keeps the listener engaged and constantly discovering new layers of meaning. The production quality of the album is another highlight. Every sound feels meticulously placed, creating a soundscape that is both immersive and expansive. The textures and tones are rich, creating a listening experience that feels almost cinematic in scope. There's a sense of space and atmosphere that envelops the listener, making the music feel alive and breathing. In conclusion, "The Fellowship of the Mystery" is a testament to Compassionizer's artistry and their ability to create music that resonates on multiple levels. It's an album that rewards repeated listens, with each playthrough revealing new details and emotions. The band's commitment to their craft is palpable, and it's exciting to see where they will go from here as they continue to evolve and refine their sound. This is a must-listen for anyone who appreciates deep, thoughtful, and emotionally charged music.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Mental Architects are a very interesting math rock band from Bulgaria, that is unfortunately nolonger active. The trio consisting of Tony Velev (guitars), Nikki Ranguelov (bass), and MaxStoimenov (drums) tackles a rhythmically complex style that is simultaneously melodic, light-hearted, and digestible. Unlike many contemporary names in the math rock scene, MA have the peculiartendency to write fun and catchy sophisticated music, as you will often hear neat riffs and grooved-out chords on their 2012 studio album 'Celebrations', which is officially their third outing. Thereis an ostensible yet subtle post-rock aftertaste all over this record, but definitely not in theform of otherworldly crescendos or extended solos. The album is pretty playful and energetic, and tomy ears, one of the few math rock collections that could make you want to... dance?Why not; after all this is a celebratory album that impresses with a vast and flourishing guitarsound, often enough relying on multiple lines working around each other (this is a strong studioproject, above all), while the bass guitar and the drums, as tasty as they are, remain lessprominent, or even a little restrained, if you will. Had the band been more fusion-oriented, therhythm section could have been more unconventional and more prone to experimentation, but MentalArchitects' music is incredibly enjoyable, nonetheless. The compositions that certainly impress meon this album are 'Spell Shelter', 'Here Is Where, Where Better' (respectively the first and secondtracks), the 7-minute-long 'Caves of Keys', which is mesmerizing, and the song called 'Meth-Rock',which appears towards the end of the album. There is a joyous warmth to the music on 'Celebrations',which will appeal to many listeners, but that album cover... it's just alright.

items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — Delirium's sixth studio album Sesta strada lungo il tempo (Sixth Road Through Time) was released in May this year, with a line-up similar to that responsible for 2015's L'Era della Menzogna, Enrico Tixi replacing drummer Alfredo Vandresi. It's not a concept album but references to the band's previous output, snapshots of time, characters and places, all create a series of linked stories embellished with a sense of Liguria and the sea.Opening with a multipart side-long track Schiavo della vilt� (Slave of Cowardice), it's obvious that the group are in full-on prog mode. The piece concerns itself with the morals of warfare through a protagonist who witnesses, and takes part in the horrors of war, knowing the acts are evil but is unable to speak out against them out of fear for what would happen to him. He reflects on leaving his lover behind as he sets off for war, and on the futility of conflict, the lives lost, never to dream, love or be free again. He finds his deeds shameful while his fellow soldiers seem to revel in the bloodshed in the name of the national flag. Musically, it fits together really well; different moods correspond to different sections and the lyrics, which recall Tremori antichi (from Lo scemo e il villaggio), are delivered with Corvaglia's dramatic vocals. Io clochard (I'm a Homeless Person) begins 'beyond the snow', blood-stained snow having featured in Schiavo della vilt�. A few bars of plaintive strings reflect the hardships of the protagonist; the dusty road and stale, mouldy bread that still tastes good, an indication that the perceived tribulations aren't unbearable. He's got his dog as a companion, time to rest and reflect, and a destination: the sea. The music primarily consists of a dense repeated phrase with a bubbly bass adding some colour, overlain with short saxophone breaks and a brief guitar solo, and guest vocalist Alice Vigo repeats the final verse in French.Il riposo del pirata (The Pirate's Rest) begins with ambient seashore sounds. Electric piano is employed in a rhythmic context, and saxophone and synthesizer weave around the vocal melody describing an old pirate in an old hammock, cradling a tankard of rum and listening to a song he can hear on the wind. Martial music indicates the final rest of the pirate and there'll be no more looting of treasure. The voices of the pirate crew can be discerned underneath Corvaglia's announcement, speaking in English: "I don't know what to do" and "I've had enough of this". Short organ sax and solos precede the final spoken verse, describing the crew celebrating the valour of the pirate on the sand where the waves bring in light foam reminiscent of freshly poured beer.Della strada il ritorno (On the Road Back) is a jazzy instrumental, beginning with string bass and piano. The piece has a real swing and there's a pleasing rhythmic complexity with Grice's saxophone soloing over the drums, bass and piano. A series of solos, energetic guitar, slower paced bass, flute, piano and sax complete the tune.Parole nel vento (Words in the Wind) has a fairly straightforward opening, before a flute riff, backed by hard rhythmic intervals, leads the song into Jethro Tull-like territory. I'm reminded of Corvaglia's track Il cerchio del comando on S.E.I. by La Maschera di Cera, which I've previously described as being like a Delirium song. Vigo shines on a lead synthesizer line that could have been performed by Keith Emerson, and following the last two vocal lines the band indulge in a blues blow out until the end of the song. While the lyrical content seems to reference both Il nome del vento ("The words thrown into the wind, who will listen?") and L'Era della Menzogna ("An ageless story made of a few lies and illusions mixed with fake freedom"), the track feels like it's pulling the strands of the four preceding stories together, creating a perfect ending.The whole album makes an enjoyable listen. It's well-crafted with a very high standard musicianship and production, expertly blending a distinct feel of past Delirium albums with an updated sound. Highly recommended.(This review originally appeared as part of a Delirium band history/album review on progblog.co.uk)

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A retrospective that deserves the attention and respect that its subject, David "Axe" Axelrod does. The only problem I have with this album is the glaring omission of his work with Julian "Cannonball" Adderley ("Mercy, Mercy, Mercy"!), the absence of anything from the two albums Capitol Records commissioned David to produce (and compose music for) by the "failing" Electric Prunes--two albums that are now recognized as leading lights of the 1960s Psychedelic era of music (and culture). Otherwise I am very happy with the attempt to raise consciousness of Axe's significant contributions to pop, jazz, and funk musics. A book should be written about this passionate, haunted, and fearless man--a true champion and loud advocate of human rights, civil rights, and care and attention to the wronged, down-trodden, dispossessed, oppressed, and marginalized.I also love the fact that there are songs of David's presented here that I'd never heard before. It could have been a double or triple album!

items.body: Review by ken_scrbrgh — There is an irony that I am considering Steve Howe's, "Beginnings," after ruminating over the four other Yes' solo albums released in 1975-1976: Howe's was the first to make its premiere. "Authentic" is the adjective I would like to employ in pondering this album almost fifty-one years after its emergence."Yesfreak" that I was back then and now, I must admit that, unlike Chris Squire's, "Fish Out of Water," I was not drawn to "Beginnings." In truth, for many years, I was seriously familiar only with Squire's album. Only since 2023, have I thoroughly come to appreciate Anderson, White, and Moraz' efforts. I would venture Howe's record emerged first in 1975 as the result of the solo work he maintained parallel to his work with Yes. I have to speculate that during the conception and initial execution of the pieces destined to yield "Beginnings," Howe chose to sing the lead vocals. Perhaps, then, as a matter of economy and facilitation, he opted to retain his lead vocal performances? If we consider 2023's, "Mirror to the Sky" and this year's, "Aurora," we encounter "successful" lead vocals from Howe on, "Unknown Place" and "Countermovement." Surely, though, in the mid-Seventies, Howe's lead vocals on his first solo album attenuated attention given to this effort.Then and now this lack of interest is unfortunate. As a generalization, "Beginnings'" compositions, instrumentality, and lyrics are effective; the poem "Doors of Sleep" by Alice Meynell sets the stage for the entire album. On "Doors of Sleep" and "Lost Symphony," the vocals are fine. With White at the drums, Howe performs all other instruments on the album opener. Perhaps the direct means of appreciating Howe's first album lies in the instrumentals "Beginnings" and "Nature of the Sea." With orchestration by Patrick Moraz, "Beginnings" certainly draws upon the "symphonic" in "prog." I would also add "chamber" and "neo-Baroque." One might consider "Beginnings" to be Howe's "answer" to the chamber orchestra on "Time and a Word." Through this piece, Howe displays his studied approach to classical guitar and to the use of the volume pedal. Although not orchestral, "The Nature of the Sea," gives us further insight into the compositional character of Steve Howe's imagination in the mid-Seventies. With an ensemble of players found only on this album's song (Malcolm Bennett, bass, David Oberle, drums, and Graeme Taylor, guitar), Howe exemplifies the "ebb and flow" of an ocean, rendering a microcosm of "Tales from the Topographic Oceans."Considering "Will 'O' The Wisp," one can visualize Howe, Moraz, and White in the studio contemporaneously with "Relayer" or shortly thereafter. With Moraz' mellotron, Howe parallels the ephemeral character of love's relationships with the paranormal, "Will 'O' The Wisp."Perhaps "Lost Symphony" is the truly solid, single piece on "Beginnings." Here, we venture into jazz with the saxophone and productive lead vocals by Howe. As with "Will 'O' The Wisp," Moraz and White support."Beginnings" provides us with an authentic window into the creative mind of Steve Howe in the mid-Seventies. For those of us who have been given the "gift of time," we can perceive the origins of the narrative of Howe's musical journey.

items.body: Review by Atri Isla — Images and Words is my‑favorite album. On this record, Dream Theater perfectly blends progressive ideas with heartfelt emotional expression. The instrumental arrangements are intricate yet full of beauty. Pull Me Under is a progressive‑metal track with pop‑oriented qualities. I am deeply impressed by the atmosphere built within its intro.Another Day delivers magnificent emotional expression, and its solo is absolutely breathtaking.Metropolis Pt.1 "The Miracle and the Sleeper" is a brilliant narrative piece. It lays out the outline and key hints for the whole Metropolis story, which later inspired the creation of Metropolis Pt. 2.The closing track Learning to Live, in my opinion, is the most underrated song on the album. James LaBrie's vocal performance here is simply stunning.To sum up, Images and Words pioneered a brand‑new creative paradigm for progressive metal and marks the starting‑point of modern progressive metal. Its power of emotional expression stands nearly unrivaled among works of this genre.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — La Maschera Di Cera offers three expansive tracks that, much like a candle flame, burn slowly, creating the illusion that the wax remains in place rather than dripping down. Il Tempo Millenario, the first of the suites, opens with keyboards taking the lead, backed by a powerful bass-and-drums tandem reminiscent of the Yes lineup featuring Squire, Wakeman, and Bruford. Later, as Alessandro Corvaglia sings in his native tongue, accompanied only by acoustic guitar and Martin Grice's flute, the music shifts to an intimate atmosphere that embraces Italian tradition. Yet another side of that tradition also emerges: one defined by intricate rhythms evoking unexplored, inhospitable landscapes, driven by keyboard lines that resemble choral vocals punctuated by the drums.When the saxophone enters, also played by Martin Grice, the sound takes on not only a jazzy feel but also a dark quality through the keyboards; the bass and piano then come to the fore amidst a shifting, atmospheric soundscape... much like the very shape of melting wax: capricious and unpredictable.There is a rock edge to Alessandro Corvaglia's voice that complements the music's solemnity and its grandiose keyboard arrangements, which later take on a darker tone through the electric clavichord and electric guitar, achieving operatic atmospheres akin to Banco del Mutuo Soccorso. Much like that band, a free-jazz passage follows, reworking the same melody in a different key; and although Alessandro is not a tenor like Francesco Di Giacomo, he rises to the challenge admirably.Il Cerchio del Comando opens with keyboards reminiscent of the Van Der Graaf Generator that made a triumphant comeback in the 2000s as a trio. The flute then introduces a more pastoral feel, though Alessandro's vocals infuse the track with a groove blending rock, funk, and soul, recalling the acoustic side of bands like Delirium, complete with flute and Mellotron. In fact, Martin Grice had been in Delirium in the 70s."Vacuo Senso" has an overwhelming opening; following the Mellotron, bass, and flute, it erupts with saxophone and electric guitar until keyboard interludes suspend the melody, creating a strange sense of oxygen deprivation, as if one were set adrift in deep space. Echoes of King Crimson, Van der Graaf, and opera are present, yet when the guitar and piano enter, delicate counterpoints, reminiscent of Premiata Forneria Marconi, wrap the dark universe in silk and bathe it in light. The piano and bass move forward warmly, crafting an endearing melody that proves the band's ability to evoke diverse modos, much like the hues wax takes on once it dries. As if that weren't enough, an improvised jazz passage follows featuring bass, piano, and drums; it retains a melodic core, and the addition of the saxophone completes the picture, including a nod to John Coltrane's "My Favorite Things."The surprises keep coming, as a keyboard solo takes center stage, reminiscent of a Canterbury-scene album or a blend of Soft Machine and Supersister, before the saxophone steers the jazz-rock sound into full-on rock territory (a feat they mastered even without guitars). Then, an atonal keyboard passage shifts into piano, heralding the conclusion of a magnificent work; it evokes the feel of a Genesis suite, carrying a melancholic, reflective air, like a retrospective look at events past, leaving no space unfilled, much like light bouncing off windowpanes after the candle has been extinguished.

items.body: And all this time I’ve been hurting for you Whatever I tried, it didn’t matter And all of my heart has been aching for you Gave all of my love – did it even matter? There is something fitting about Jonny Pierce opening his new label Abysmal Records with a song about emotional nullification. The Drums have spent fifteen years turning romantic injury into bright, economical pop, yet It Didn’t Matter, a collaboration with Mareux, carries a colder sense of aftermath. Its title lands with the bluntness of a verdict delivered after the argument has ended, when language has been exhausted, and the abandoned person is left to rearrange the evidence. Mareux’s presence is immediately legible. Aryan Ashtiani supplies synthesizers that glide with severe elegance, placing Pierce’s voice inside a glassy architecture of drum-machine momentum and bruised pop chords straight off the 80s pop charts. The production remains clean without becoming sterile; each element has room to move, while the song’s forward motion suggests somebody walking quickly through a city to avoid calling the person they are trying to forget. Pierce sings with the fragile directness that has long defined The Drums, though age has added a finer grain to his delivery. Foolishness, need, and disbelief are presented without disguise. The song describes someone trapped in the aftermath of an unequal relationship, still longing for a partner who pushed them away without releasing them. Hurt, ashamed, and angry at themselves for needing love, they question whether their devotion, sacrifice, and enduring pain ever meant anything to the person they loved. Pierce describes the session in unusually personal terms: “Not since writing my earliest music has a song come together so effortlessly. Whenever that happens, it makes me feel certain the song was meant to exist -that it needed to be here, for all of us. Mareux’s synthesizer wizardry threw me back to my teenage years, when almost everything I listened to was synthesizer-based music, especially synth-pop. His sounds, textures, and perfect pop chord changes reminded me of the soundtrack to such a tender time in my life – when I was desperate for love but just couldn’t find it, and synthesizers became the soundtrack to my sadness. This one is for those of us who keep banging our heads against the wall of another heart, only to be given nothing in return.” The collaboration grants Mareux increasing space to move beyond the viral mythology of his Cure cover, “The Perfect Girl,” showcasing him as a composer whose precise synthesizer skills elevate another artist’s songwriting and emotion. A disciplined bassline, succinct percussion, and sighing keys anchor Pierce’s confession here, letting the melody carry the emotional weight that the production keeps in elegant balance. Watch the visualizer for It Didn’t Matter below: It Didn’t Matter‘s autobiographical charge belongs to a lineage of synth-pop where polished surfaces intensify private collapse, but Pierce and Ashtiani avoid empty period detail. Their shared instincts meet in the space between romantic candour and formal restraint, producing a track that feels immediate without sounding disposable. As the first entry in a six-month series of collaborations, it gives Abysmal Records a persuasive opening statement. More importantly, it suggests that Pierce’s next phase may be built through exchange rather than isolation. It Didn’t Matter turns rejection into motion, carrying its unanswered question forward with poise, clarity and a quietly devastating hook. Catch Mareux live this autumn: 09/19 — Santa Ana, CA — Observatory Festival Grounds with AFI, Kumo 99, and L.A. items.body: Hey pals, we’re back! Thanks for sticking with us through some post-Terminus hiatus action, we needed a couple of days to rest and recoup before jumping back into the regular posting schedule, this short week notwithstanding. And hey, the upside of all of this is that we’re unusually amped to dig in on some new releases, the after-effects of seeing a ton of great music (as outlined on last week’s podcast in excruciating detail). That’s a good lead-in to this stacked edition of Tracks! Bestial Mouths doing the Bestial Mouths thing Boy Harsher, “Hard Beat” We’ve been following Boy Harsher since around the release of the first EP, and seeing them become such an enormous phenomenon with legions of fans and scads of imitators has been something of a trip. With that said, it was obvious that the duo couldn’t (and more importantly, wouldn’t) just rehash their most popular sounds and songs on their next LP, which is where “Hard Beat” comes in. Yeah, you can def hear classic BH in it, but you’re also getting a healthy dose of their interest in electropop and some more smooth and even housey vibes that differentiate it. We’ll certainly be discussing Get Mean when it drops in September, stay tuned. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Bestial Mouths, “Conjure” Bestial Mouths have not-so-quietly become of the true stalwarts of modern darkwave, avoiding many of the broader trends and following their own gnarly, uncomfortable and often very fraught muse. The forthcoming album Dead Lines is produced entirely by band member Brant Showers, and you can definitely hear aspects of his sound design from AAIMON and SØLVE in “Conjure”, but it’s entirely in service of project mastermind Lynette Cerezo’s powerful, terrifying voice and presence. Stunning cut, and no doubt a precursor for more ill winds yet to come. DEAD LINES by Bestial Mouths Purest Form, “Animal” LA trio Purest Form look to be shooting for the moon with their forthcoming EP on Dais. Lead single “Animal” is a bracing mix of super-processed metal chug and 90s electronica at large, a formula that’ll be catnip to rivets of a certain generation still pining after quality KMFDM releases, but will likely offer fresh contrasts and new avenues for younger kids still finding their bearings in emergent apocalypses. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM Ratio Strain, “Exorcism (Iszoloscope remix)” Hot on the heels of her excellent performance at Terminus, we have a new single from San Diego’s Ratio Strain. The lineup of remixers taking on the track “Exorcism” reflects a lot of Ratio Strain’s specific take on modern instrumental industrial and rhythmic noise, emphasizing dancefloor appeal and big textures in equal measure. Hence why you get some acid chaos from Hex Wolves, bass leaning sound design from Zer0signal, and a hot dose of inhuman ambience from Iszoloscope, the grandmaster of that particular sound. Exorcism: Possessed by Ratio Strain The Axiom Divide, “The Halls Of Amenti” The Axiom Divide is a brand-spanking new project, but look beneath the surface (as in the throwback cyber-mapping of Egyptian mysteries on the album art) and things might be a bit more familiar. Threads of frontman Jay Tye’s work in long-tenued COP act Soil & Eclipse can definitely be teased out in this melodic and ethereal blend of futurepop, synthpop, and Euro styled electro at large. The Halls of Amenti : Remixes by The Axiom Divide Anaxia, “Laser Star” A new side project from Rich Oddie of Canadian legends Orphx and Alex Pi, the taster cuts from Anaxia’s first EP speak to a controlled mastery of mood and mode. Finding commonalities between EBM, synthpunk, and post-punk and boiling their rhythmic elements down to the core, the pair flesh that skeleton out with anxious pads and squalls, taking the core elements of minimal wave to paradoxically smothering excess.
